title: Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
alternative_titles: Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
Characteristics
description: Shaftesbury's collected philosophical miscellany, binding together his earlier treatises on virtue, enthusiasm, wit, and the moral sense with meditations, maxims, and letters. It set out the argument that moral approval rests on a natural sentiment rather than on divine law or self-interest, and that ridicule is the test of a healthy, sociable mind.
plot_or_argument: The volume assembles several distinct essays: an inquiry showing virtue to consist in the balance of social affections, an enquiry into the nature of enthusiasm and superstition, a defence of wit and freedom of thought, a rhapsodic dialogue on the moralists, and meditations on the self and on human life. Shaftesbury argues that every creature's affections divide into natural, social, and selfish, and that virtue is the right system of these when guided by reflection. A 'test or sieve' of ridicule is offered for opinions about religion, since what can bear being ill-used is likely true. The miscellaneous thoughts and maxims draw the portrait of the accomplished 'gentleman' whose virtue, wit, and taste are one politeness. The whole is presented not as a system but as a character of the author's own mind, inviting free censure and examination.
narrative_structure: An artfully ordered miscellany rather than a single argument: treatises of different dates are framed by advertisements, letters, and a self-memoir, so that the reader encounters one continuing intelligence under several genres.
literary_form: collected philosophical essays, treatises, dialogue, and maxims
meter_and_prosody: Prose of epigrammatic density, mixing periodic balance with abrupt sententious brevity; the maxims compress moral observation into pointed, often antithetical sentences.
historical_context: Published in London in 1711 as the party war over the Sacramental Tests made toleration and enthusiasm live issues, and self-published by its author without a dedicated patron. It gathered the separately printed works of 1699-1710 and at once became a focus of the controversy over natural theology that Toland, Collins, and their opponents were conducting.
literary_significance: It supplied the eighteenth century's vocabulary of moral sense, politeness, wit, and enthusiasm and shaped Hutcheson, Hume, and the British aesthetic tradition; its theory of ridicule and its ideal of the accomplished character are central documents of the English Enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 3 vols. in 1 vol., 1711, printed for the author and sold by R. Gosling and A. Bell; a much-altered edition with additions appeared in 1732, edited after Shaftesbury's death with the help of J. A. T. Des Maizeaux. The standard scholarly text is the edition by Lawrence E. Klein (Cambridge, 1999).

title: Sensus Communis: An Essay on Wit and Humour
alternative_titles: Sensus Communis, an Essay on Wit and Humour
description: Shaftesbury's essay on wit, written as a friendly critique of Anthony Collins's Essay Concerning the Use of Reason and issued the same year as the Letter Concerning Enthusiasm. It proposes ridicule as the proper test of wit and of whatever claims assent, and distinguishes true raillery, which supports sociability and liberty of thought, from the spleen and ignorance of the mere witling.
plot_or_argument: The essay opens on the character of a book and the conditions of free examination, then passes to an anatomy of wit and humour, classifying wits by their governing humour. Shaftesbury insists that ridicule, like reason, must be exercised freely and without fear, since a doctrine or religion that cannot endure to be ill-used deserves to be. He distinguishes genuine raillery, addressed to opinions and manners, from personal abuse, and traces modern wit to a mixture of the fine and the humorous. The argument closes with a defence of good manners in raillery and an appeal to common sense as the public standard of the ridiculous.
narrative_structure: A single discursive essay in loose epistolary form, moving from the conditions of free enquiry through a classification of wits to the doctrine of ridicule as test.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, pointed prose in the manner of a letter to a friend, rich in distinctions, short definitions, and barbed asides; passages of rhythmic tripartite enumeration give it the feel of spoken raillery.
historical_context: Printed in 1709 amid the freethinking debates opened by Collins and Toland, and written in dialogue with the author of A Discourse of the Liberty of the Press, whose press Shaftesbury praises while disagreeing with his conclusion. It forms part of what became the Characteristics.
literary_significance: It gave the century its most influential account of ridicule as a criterion of truth and civility, directly conditioning Addison's papers, Pope's doctrine of wit, and later theories of humour and the comic.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1709, printed for the author and sold by R. Gosling; reprinted within the Characteristics, 1711. The text was revised for the 1732 edition.

title: The Moralists, a Philosophical Rhapsody
alternative_titles: The Moralists: A Rhapsody
description: Shaftesbury's platonizing dialogue on natural theology and the happiness of virtue, first printed in the third volume of the Characteristicks and issued separately in the same year. Over a day's walk through the fields near Hampstead, the young Philocles is led by the accomplished Theocles to behold the system of the universe and the interior moral system that mirrors it.
plot_or_argument: Philocles, a youth fresh from reading the moralists, meets Theocles and Crantor in the meadows near Hampstead and asks whether virtue alone is happy. Theocles replies first by an ironical panegyric in the style of the sophists, then seriously, rising through an account of the affections and the moral sense to the 'rhapsody' proper: the visible scene of nature becomes the occasion for the vision of the whole system, its administrative god, and the self-enjoying blessedness of a mind in harmony with it. The dialogue ends with Philocles convinced that virtue, happiness, and the contemplation of the universal system are one.
narrative_structure: An occasional dialogue framed as a 'rhapsody': reported walk and conversation in a single day, climaxing in an extended inspired passage of natural theology.
principal_characters: Philocles; Theocles; Crantor
meter_and_prosody: Animated prose dialogue with dramatic description, rising in the closing rhapsody to a deliberately periodic, almost poetic cadence of accumulation and apostrophe.
historical_context: Composed in the 1690s from material in Shaftesbury's Journals of the Meridian and printed in 1709, when deistic natural theology was being hotly contested; its vision of the system draws on the Cambridge Platonists and on the new cosmology of the Royal Society age.
literary_significance: It is the most accomplished piece of Shaftesbury's prose art and a key text of eighteenth-century natural theology and the aesthetics of the sublime system; its rhapsody anticipated the nature-contemplation of Thomson, Akenside, and the Romantic moment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1709 as the third treatise of the third volume of the Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times, with a separate title-page; also reprinted separately in that year. Text as revised in the 1732 edition.

title: An Inquiry Concerning Virtue or Merit
alternative_titles: An Inquiry Concerning Virtue, or Merit
An Essay upon the Conduct and Passions of the Mind
description: Shaftesbury's foundational treatise of moral sense theory, first circulated privately in 1699 as An Essay upon the Conduct and Passions of the Mind and given substantially its final form in the Characteristics. It argues that moral distinction arises from a natural sentiment responding to the balance of the affections, not from law, contract, or self-interest.
plot_or_argument: The Inquiry analyses the mind into natural, social, and selfish affections and shows that a reflective sense approves the system in which the social affections hold due proportion to the rest. Virtue is thus the right balance of a secondary, reflective nature, and the sense of it is as immediate as the sense of beauty. Shaftesbury refutes at length the egoism of Hobbes and the voluntarism of Pufendorf, arguing that obligation cannot be grounded in self-love or in will alone. He extends the account to a 'theology of the moral sense', showing the same harmony in the universal system, and closes with a defence of the claim that virtue is the interest of the species and of each person within it.
narrative_structure: A sustained analytical treatise in two parts, moving from the division of the affections through the definition of virtue to the confutation of opponents and the enlarged cosmological conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Tight, reflective prose built on numbered distinctions and recurring triads (affections, senses, systems), with a tendency toward balanced periodic closers.
historical_context: Written in the shadow of Locke's Essay and of the Locke-Filiimerde-Stillingfleet controversies, and shaped by Shaftesbury's own Journals; its 1699 essay version circulated among the Whig wits before its authorized appearance in the Characteristics of 1711.
literary_significance: It founded the British sentimentalism of Hutcheson, Hume, and Adam Smith and set the terms for a century of debate whether moral distinction is sentiment or reason.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First printed as An Essay upon the Conduct and Passions of the Mind. With a Letter to a Friend concerning the Enthusiasticks, 1699 (circulated in copy, not published for sale); the revised Inquiry first appeared in volume 1 of the Characteristics, London, 1711. Publication date given as 1711 for the authorized text under this title.

title: The Fable of the Bees
alternative_titles: The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits
The Grumbling Hive, or Knaves Turned Honest
description: Mandeville's paradox poem and prose commentary, developing the thesis that private vices - luxury, pride, avarice, sensuality - are publicly beneficial because they set trade, ingenuity, and civility in motion. The first edition paired the 1705 poem 'The Grumbling Hive' with an enquiring essay; the enlarged edition of 1723-29 added a second fable, part of a play, and an extended discussion of the moral origins of virtue.
plot_or_argument: A hive of prosperous bees, 'full of knaves', thrives on fraud, luxury, and emulation until a divine reformer makes them honest; virtue then starves trade, and the hive falls to a despicable abject state, the moral being that neither saints nor knaves can make a 'hiv' well governed. The prose essays that follow argue, paradox by paradox, that the most corrupt societies may be the most flourishing, that honour and shame are artificial engines of social cooperation, and that self-denial for its own sake is a sophism. Mandeville's later Defence and Enquiry extend the argument against 'virtue without renunciation' and against the church's account of moral self-love, distinguishing the 'fine gloss' of virtue from its real, self-interested sources.
narrative_structure: A short allegorical poem in heroic couplets followed by increasingly long prose essays, a defence, and enquiries; the second edition added a further fable, a dramatic poem 'The Grumbling Hive' turned into a play, and an examination of the reviewer.
principal_characters: the bees of the hive; the God of the hive; Mandeville as essayist and respondent
literary_form: allegorical poem with prose philosophical essays
meter_and_prosody: The fable is written in tight, dry heroic couplets of iambic pentameter in the manner of Auguean didactic satire; the commentary is plain, colloquial argumentative prose.
historical_context: Developed from the 1705 poem printed for a Whig club, published as the Fable in 1714 and greatly enlarged in 1723-29, when it provoked formal presentments by the Grand Jury of Middlesex and a flood of replies; it belongs to the debates over luxury, commerce, and national decline opened by the 1720s economic writings.
literary_significance: It is the century's most provocative contribution to the luxury debate, a decisive influence on Hume, Adam Smith, and the ideas of unintended social order, and a landmark of paradoxical prose satire.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: The Fable of the Bees; or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits first published London, 1714 (for B. Bell and others), containing 'The Grumbling Hive' (first printed 1705) and 'An Enquiry into the Happiness of Their Kingdoms'; the second, enlarged edition appeared in 1723-24 with Part II, the Defence, and the Enquiry, with a 'Further Reflections' added 1729. The standard edition is Kay F. Ewers's (Oxford, 2014).

title: A Modest Defence of Publick Stews
alternative_titles: A Modest Defence of a Publick Stew
A Modest Defence of Publick Stews; or, An Essay Upon Whoring
description: Mandeville's notorious polemical pamphlet proposing licensed public brothels ('stews') as a remedy for the social miseries of clandestine prostitution, seduction, and venereal disease. Its calm institutional logic, applied to the most censurable subject, makes it both a piece of social planning and an experiment in the rhetoric of Mandevillian paradox.
plot_or_argument: The essay first states the problem in terms of the failure of law and morality to suppress private prostitution, which spreads disease and ruins women and families unseen. It then proposes regulated stews, arguing by analogy with the management of the poor, the army, and the taxes that what cannot be prevented can be supervised, taxed, and made innocent of its worst harms. Objections from religion, modesty, and policy are enumerated and answered one by one with the pamphlet's signature deflating arithmetic of consequences. The conclusion holds that a legislature which consults 'the Nature of the Beast' rather than its ideals will secure public health and quiet where sermons have failed.
narrative_structure: A single sustained argumentative pamphlet: statement of the mischief, proposal, systematic confutation of objections, and practical peroration.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, reasoningly colloquial prose,ironically modelled on the tones of a modest proposal, with lists of objections and answers driving its rhythm.
historical_context: Published in London in 1724 with a letter to the Grand Jury of Middlesex, in the immediate aftermath of the Fable's prosecution and of the 'Mauduit' affair; it engages the same licensed-immorality debate that the Reformation of Manners societies and the Gin Age produced.
literary_significance: It remains Mandeville's boldest test of whether public policy should reason from things as they are rather than as piety wishes them, and a key document of eighteenth-century debates about prostitution, regulation, and the language of projects.
attribution_notes: Attributed without serious doubt to Mandeville, who signed related material and defended the pamphlet's premises within his own system; the imprint does not name him.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1724, as A Modest Defence of Publick Stews: or, An Essay Upon Whoring, containing a letter to the Grand Jury; reprinted within the Various Issues of Mandeville's works and in F. B. Kaye's edition of the essays. Some copies also carry the designation second edition, 1724.

title: Christianity Not Mysterious
alternative_titles: Christianity Not Mysterioues; or, A Treatise Shewing, That there is nothing in the Gospel contrary to Reason, or above it
description: Toland's founding tract of the deist controversy, arguing that the gospel contains nothing contrary to reason or above it and that mystery in religion is a clerical invention imported from neoplatonism and popery. It insists that what is not universally knowable is not universally necessary, and so strips the Christian scheme of its esoteric hierarchy of truths.
plot_or_argument: Toland first defines the terms of religious language and shows Scripture to address all rational capacities, containing nothing contradictory and nothing whose knowledge is required but withheld. He then traces the mystery system to the neoplatonic and Roman corruption of primitive Christianity, in which priests reserved hidden meanings to themselves. Against the plea of divine condescension to human weakness, he argues that a revelation for all mankind must be intelligible to all. Reason is made the ground of assent even to revealed propositions, since the evidence of miracles must itself be rationally weighed. The conclusion is that Christianity is a reasonable, plain institution whose mysteries are only things not yet understood.
narrative_structure: A single argumentative treatise in two discourses with a preliminary defence of its propositions, advancing by definition, historical confutation, and theological conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Lean, polemical prose of sustained syllogistic pressure, divided into numbered propositions and scholastic distinctions in ironic contrast to their content.
historical_context: Published the year after Locke's Reasonableness of Christianity and drawing on his unitarian temper, it was ordered burnt by the hangman and denounced in the Irish House of Lords, where Toland sat; it opened the chain of deist claims that Collins, Tindal, and Morgan would extend.
literary_significance: It set the agenda of the English deist controversy for a generation and made the intelligibility of revelation the central question of natural and revealed religion; its rationalist criterion became the foil for Butler's Analogy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1696; a second edition with a defence against the Bishop of Winchester's reply appeared in 1697, and a third in 1702. Condemned by the Irish parliament, with an order for burning, 1697.

title: Letters to Serena
alternative_titles: Letters to Serena, Occasioned in a Stay in France
description: Toland's Spinozist-tinged philosophical letters, written during and after a stay in France, which develop a necessitarian, materialist account of mind, matter, and the eternity of the species. The letters to his correspondent Serena are prefixed by a discourse on the eastern philosophy arguing that European learning derived from the East.
plot_or_argument: The prefatory discourse maintains that philosophy migrated east-to-west and that the Greeks learned from barbarian sages, demoting the miracle of Greek originality. The letters then argue that motion is essential to matter, so that an immaterial, unmoved mover is unintelligible; thought likewise arises in organized matter, and the mind is not a separable substance. From this Toland draws the eternity of the universe and of the species of creatures, against creation out of nothing and against the doctrine of a naturally mortal soul, reading Genesis as a natural history of this world only. Personal immortality is dissolved into the perpetuity of nature, and religion is reinterpreted as the homage of a mind that contemplates the whole.
narrative_structure: A sequence of familiar letters on connected philosophical topics, framed by a prefatory historical discourse.
principal_characters: Serena (the addressee); the writer
meter_and_prosody: Supple epistolary prose, argumentative but conversational, with long distinctions worked out through examples and retorts.
historical_context: Written after Toland's 1707-08 continental visit, where he studied the reception of Spinoza on the continent, and published amid the post-Clarke debates on the soul and on the sufficiency of reason.
literary_significance: It introduced a Spinozist necessitarianism into English philosophical letters and became a standard citation in the pantheist scares of the century; its eastern-philosophy thesis early globalized the history of ideas.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1709 (for J. Rivington); parts of the correspondence with Ancillon appeared in the Acta Eruditorum before collection. Reprinted in Toland's Collected Works, 1718.

title: A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty
alternative_titles: A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Liberty
description: Anthony Collins's libertarian manifesto, the first sustained English argument that liberty is a power of acting according to the determination of the will, and that necessity so understood is compatible with, indeed the condition of, freedom. It attacks the doctrine of liberty of indifference as unintelligible and self-contradictory.
plot_or_argument: Collins defines liberty as a power of acting according to the will's determination, and argues that every act of the will is determined by its object or by preceding causes. The liberty of indifference, a power to choose either way without preponderating motive, he shows to be unintelligible, since an undetermined choice would be mere chance and not agency. He then presses the moral and theological consequences: a determined will can still be free in the only sense that matters for praise, blame, and law. The closing chapters answer the objection that necessity destroys religion and morality, and defend the compatibility scheme against its clerical opponents.
narrative_structure: A short treatise in ten chapters: definitions, the history of the controversy, the confutation of indifference, the affirmative argument, and replies to moral and religious objections.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, terse argumentative prose with scholastic distinctions handled lightly; the chapters close on sharp either/or dilemmas.
historical_context: Published in 1717 during the noise made by Collins's earlier Essay on the Use of Reason and his dispute with Clarke, and part of the freethinking campaign that Hume's later writings on liberty and necessity would answer.
literary_significance: It fixed the vocabulary of the liberty-necessity debate in English for half a century, providing the hard libertarian position against which Hutcheson, Hume, and Reid defined their own schemes.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1717 (for A. Bettesworth and J. Clarke); a second edition followed the same year with material against William Wollaston's objections, and a third in 1727.

title: An Essay Concerning the Use of Reason
alternative_titles: A Discourse of the Use of Reason in Learning and Religion
description: Anthony Collins's early rationalist treatise arguing that reason is the adequate judge of all revelation and that nothing can be believed on authority that is contrary to or beyond clear perception. It generalizes the scriptural rule of trial by reason into a standard by which every pretended revelation must stand or fall.
plot_or_argument: The Essay first settles what a proposition must be before it can be assented to, insisting that ideas must be clear and their agreement or disagreement perceived. Applying this to revelation, Collins argues that we can know a revelation to be divine only by the same rational evidence by which we know anything, so that what seems contrary to knowledge must be rejected, whatever its pretences. Mystery pleaded as super-rational assent is shown to collapse into either plain nonsense or a concealed contradiction. He then answers the argument from the shortness of reason's sight and from the necessity of a divine commission, and concludes that faith is rational assent, not a surrender of judgment.
narrative_structure: A systematic essay in numbered chapters: theory of proportion and assent, application to revelation, confutation of mystery and of the standard replies, and a closing vindication of rational faith.
meter_and_prosody: Dry, closely reasoned lockean prose with numbered definitions and repeated test questions driving the advance.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1707, it provoked Samuel Clarke's Defence of the Natural Instability of Humane Reason (1707) and Collins's own Reply (1708), and supplied the terms on which the Christian evidence controversy continued into the 1720s.
literary_significance: It is the boldest pre-deist statement of the ratio principle, the text that made freethinking a named intellectual cause and set the agenda to which Butler and the evidentialists answered.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; authorship established by Clarke's reply naming Collins and by contemporary attribution.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1707, printed for William Reynolds; second edition with a Reply to Clarke, 1708; reprinted in Collins's Collected Works, 1788.

title: A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion
description: Collins's historical-critical pamphlet, treating Christianity as a this-worldly political phenomenon whose grounds lie in Jewish messianic expectation and whose reasons for assent are those of the Jewish religion it answered. Published amid the Woolston trials, it provoked a swarm of replies and a parliamentary outrage.
plot_or_argument: Collins argues that the Jews expected a temporal Messiah, and that the first preachers addressed purely political hopes shaped by that expectation. On this account Christianity's rise is explained by causes within history: a deluded expectation later corrected by an allegorical reading after the failure of the temporal kingdom. The spiritualizing interpretation, he suggests, is a shift that saved the sect from extinction and made prophecy serve whatever happened. He closes with a proposal: the true Messiah remains to come, and the grounds of Christian assent, being historical and political, are weaker than those of the Jewish religion they displaced.
narrative_structure: A compact single discourse moving from the political state of the Jews, through the causes of Christianity's rise, to the allegorizing solution and a concluding query about the true Messiah.
meter_and_prosody: Level, deadpan argumentative prose, with startling conclusions reached through a series of apparently neutral historical enquiries.
historical_context: Published in 1724, the same year as Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation and in the shadow of Woolston's libel trial; the House of Commons resolved to prosecute the author, making it a cause celebre of the deist decade.
literary_significance: It is the most political of the deist attacks, turning the evidences inside out by explaining religion from the interests it served, and a decisive provocation for the historical and moral apologetics of the following decades.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1724; a second edition with an Appendix appeared the same year and a third in 1725; replies included those by Benjamin Hoadly and Thomas Sherlock. Reprinted in Collins's Collected Works, 1788.

title: The Rights of the Christian Church Asserted
alternative_titles: The Rights of the Christian Church: with a Civil and Historical Account of the Tithes and Revenue of Priests
description: Tindal's Erastian controversy treatise, arguing from scriptural and historical grounds that the primitive church required no endowments, no clergy as a separate order, and no coercion, and that the modern established priesthood had repealed the very religion it professed. It turned the deist critique outward onto the political economy of the church.
plot_or_argument: Tindal first proves from Scripture that the apostles intended no permanent clerical order with temporal power, and that the law of Moses, whose ceremonial was temporary, was the model of a church supported by voluntary maintenance. He then traces the rise of tithes, patronage, and ecclesiastical jurisdiction to human constitutions and imperial policy, showing the clergy's claim of divine right to be historically fraudulent. Argument from the nature of spiritual advantage follows: religion that requires wealth and coercion has repealed its own principles. The conclusion demands a return to the primitive pattern and threatens the temporal basis of the established church.
narrative_structure: A controversial treatise in two long parts of cumulative proof: scriptural demonstration, then historical confutation of the clergy's title, with an appendix of authorities.
meter_and_prosody: Dense citation-heavy prose, patristic and canon-law authorities stacked in long trains, with a plain republican bluntness of tone.
historical_context: Published in the last years of Queen Anne's reign amid the Sacheverell frenzy and high-church assaults on toleration, it went through several rapid editions, was answered by dozens of divines, and was ordered burnt by the Commons in 1715.
literary_significance: It moved the deist controversy from epistemology to institutional history, became the standard handbook of Erastian and anticlerical argument for decades, and shaped Hume's later church histories.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1706; second edition 1708 with a defence against William Wake; third edition 1709; the long-running dispute with the clergy continued through editions to 1722.

title: Christianity as Old as the Creation
alternative_titles: The Gospel a Republication of the Law of Nature
description: Tindal's mature deist statement, the fullest argument that true religion is nothing but the law of nature and must therefore be as old and as universal as creation. Its ironical appendix, the Character of a Low-Church Deist, turned the controversy into a satire on party divinity.
plot_or_argument: Tindal argues that God's religion, being designed for all rational creatures, must be uniform, intelligible, and proportioned to the nature He gave them; therefore the moral law written at creation is the whole gospel. What is called revelation can only republication and commentary: nature's religion, known by the equal light of reason, is the touchstone of every pretence to supernatural religion. The duties of the law of nature, justice, benevolence, sobriety, and piety, are the only terms of acceptance, and no positive institution can add to them. The appended Dialogue of the Dead and Character of the Low-Church Deist satirize the clergy's treatment of mystery, authority, and party.
narrative_structure: A single systematic treatise followed by burlesque dialogues and a character sketch, so that serious natural religion closes in comic warfare.
meter_and_prosody: Amplified argumentative prose, heavily periodic and repetitive for emphasis; the appendices take the lighter manner of dialogue and character writing.
historical_context: Published in the deist flush of 1729-32, the year after Berkeley's Alciphron and in the teeth of the Convocation controversy over blasphemy; it drew more than a hundred replies, Butler's Analogy among the most considered.
literary_significance: It is the summation of English deism, the text from which the movement's later critics and its American heirs alike took their definitions, and the standing provocation to every theology of supernatural religion in the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1730, printed for and sold by the author and others; second edition with additions 1731, third 1733; many replies, including those by Benjamin Brown, John Rogers, and William Law.

title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
alternative_titles: The Practical Series of a Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
description: William Law's great devotional conduct book, teaching a rule of universal devotion by which every common action, business, and hour of the day is turned into prayer. It argues that religion is not a set of duties but the whole temper of a life resigned to God's will.
plot_or_argument: Law first grounds devotion in the Gospel's own rules for ordinary conduct, then shows how the daily offices, work, meals, social hours, sleep, and sickness may each be sanctified by a fixed temper of resignation. Through portraits of worldly wise men, women of quality, the miser, the politician, and the clergyman, he proves that everything admirable in politeness is a poor counterfeit of devotion. The second movement directs the inward life: the love of God as the sole motive, the renunciation of self-will, and the sacramental use of the world. It closes with the famous counsel that a man must be a saint or wretch, and a moving description of the devout life as one hour of continuous offering.
narrative_structure: Two-part conduct treatise: doctrinal direction and rule of life, interwoven with a gallery of moral characters and closing meditations.
meter_and_prosody: A grave, rhythmic, iteratively clause-balanced prose, built on scriptural paraphrase and moral paradox; its solemn cadences were much admired and much parodied.
historical_context: Written in the quiet of Kings Clipston after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment over the nonjurors' question, and published in 1729 when deist controversy had made practical Christianity a contested idea; Johnson, Wesley, and later Newman counted it formative.
literary_significance: The most influential English devotional prose of the century between Ken and the tractarians, a standard of Anglican spiritual direction and a school of style for Samuel Johnson and many readers of the evangelical revival.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1729 (for S. Bray); early editions were often in two volumes with the Practical Series; reprinted constantly through the century; the standard modern edition is David J. P. Coupland and John R. Spinelli (Classics of Spirituality, 1990).

title: The Spirit of Prayer
alternative_titles: The Spirit of Prayer, or the Soul rising out of the Vanity of Time
The Spirit of Prayer in Three Parts
description: Law's mystical treatise on prayer as the breath of the inward soul, opposing the formal 'prayers of the mouth' to the ceaseless spirit of devotion. Part I appeared in 1733 and Parts II and III followed in 1734, extending the argument into a theology of the believer's constant intercourse with God.
plot_or_argument: Law argues that the Christian life is essentially a spirit and disposition, of which vocal prayers are only the shell; true prayer is the soul's ascending sense of dependence and love. He shows from Scripture and the Lord's Prayer why a form of words is nothing without the wants, humours, and temper it expresses. The later parts work out the practice: the universal, unceasing offering of common life, prayer as the soul rising out of the vanity of time into eternity, and the believer's participation in the intercession of Christ. Formal religion and the love of the world are thus exposed as the same failure of spirit.
narrative_structure: Three progressive parts, each a devotional argument from Scripture followed by practical direction and spiritual anatomy.
meter_and_prosody: Incantatory, paratactic prose of long accumulating sentences, borrowing the rhythms of law and the Psalms; the argument advances almost by cadence.
historical_context: Written after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment and under the influence of his reading of Jacob Boehme and the German mystical tradition, and published in 1733-34 when the blasphemy and Convocation controversies made inward religion a polemical subject.
literary_significance: It transmitted the language of seventeenth-century mysticism into eighteenth-century popular devotion and shaped, among others, the inward-prayer tradition that Methodism and the Oxford Movement both inherited.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1733 (Part I); Parts II and III issued 1734; often reprinted with The Spirit of Faith and The Life of a Believer. Modern edition with introduction by D. J. P. Coupland, 1984.

title: Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
alternative_titles: Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
Sermons, Founded on Several Occasions, Preached at the Rolls Chapel, in Chancery Lane
description: Butler's early sermon sequence on human nature, conscience, and the authority of reflection, preached at the Rolls in the 1720s and published as a philosophical defence of the natural constitution of moral agents. Its central claim, that conscience is by nature authoritative in man, answers Mandeville, Hobbes, and Shaftesbury at once.
plot_or_argument: Butler argues first that human nature is a system, not a heap of instincts, in which self-love and benevolence are naturally implanted and commonly coincide. Against psychological egoism he shows that particular passions have their own objects, and that pursuing them, not self, is the true path to happiness. Reflection or conscience surveys our actions and approves or disapproves with a natural authority that is one of degree as well as strength; to follow it is the case of the whole creature. The later sermons treat self-deception, the pursuit of pleasure, and the respect owing to conscience, grounding religion in the same constitution that grounds morality.
narrative_structure: A collected series of fifteen sermons with an analytical Preface, each sermon isolating one branch of the argument from human nature.
meter_and_prosody: The plain, exact, cumulative prose of the pulpit turned to analytic purpose: distinction after distinction, quietly weighted, with an unwonted precision of definition.
historical_context: Preached between 1719 and 1725 before a Rolls audience drawn from the chancery bar, amid the Mandeville and Shaftesbury debates on self-love; the sermons were published in 1726 with a Preface that became a locus classicus of moral philosophy.
literary_significance: The Preface and sermons anticipated the theories of benevolence, conscience, and authority debated by Hume, Reid, and the intuitionists, and remain the most-cited eighteenth-century text in moral philosophy besides the Treatise.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1726, for T. Bennet, in thirteen sermons; the second edition of 1729 enlarged the collection to fifteen with the sermon on the abuse of conscience; reprinted constantly through the century and several times since.

title: The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature
alternative_titles: The Analogy of Religion
The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed
description: Butler's great apologetic treatise, answering deism not by evidences but by analogy: the difficulties of revealed religion are shadowed at every point in the constitution and course of nature, so that a critic of the one must condemn the other. It was dedicated to Lord Chancellor Talbot and at once recognized as the century's most formidable defence.
plot_or_argument: Part I shows that the course of nature, governed by general laws with rewards and penalties attaching to conduct, is exactly the system deists find improbable in religion; the imperfections of human government, the mixture of good and evil, and the unknown ends of providence all reappear in the divine dispensations. Part II argues that Christianity, as a scheme of religious office and authority, answers to the same analogy of nature, and that a presumed a priori standard of what religion should be is self-defeating. A concluding appendix treats the credibility of Moses's history and the Christian dispensation as a scheme progressively developed. The cumulative moral is that the actual world and the actual religion stand or fall together.
narrative_structure: Two main parts of argument from analogy, each subdivided into chapters answering one class of objection, followed by appendices against specific critics.
meter_and_prosody: Massively circumstantial, judicious prose of balance-sheet periods, whose famous obscurity comes from the accumulation of qualifications and analogical correspondences.
historical_context: Published in 1736 when the deist controversy had reached its height with Tindal and Morgan, and when Hoadly's latitudinarianism had made the church's authority a practical question; it was the response of a preacher of the Inns of Court and future bishop.
literary_significance: It changed the terms of natural and revealed religion from evidence to analogy and constitution, dominating Anglican apologetic for a century; Gladstone and Arthur Balfour counted it decisive, and it remains a landmark of philosophy of religion.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1736, for J. and J. Paul; a second edition in the same year and a third in 1740, the later editions carrying the appended dissertations; reprinted throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and the staple of Anglican apologetic.

title: Commentaries on the Laws of England
alternative_titles: Blackstone's Commentaries
Commentaries on the Laws of England, in Four Volumes
description: Blackstone's four-volume systematization of the common law, grown from his Oxford Vinerian lectures of 1753 onward: rights of persons, rights of things, private wrongs, and public wrongs. It made English law a teachable rational science and became the most influential legal book of the English-speaking world.
plot_or_argument: Volume I narrates the rise of the laws, the kingdom's constitutional structure, and the rights of persons, from royal prerogative and parliamentary independence to domestic relations. Volume II reduces property, tenure, inheritance, and title to an intelligible historical grammar. Volume III treats civil wrongs and remedies, wrongs to things, and the law of actions. Volume IV defines crimes, their justifications and extenuations, and the machinery of public justice from arrest to pardon. Throughout, Blackstone presents the common law as a repository of collective wisdom, mild in its proportion of punishments and jealous of liberty, though later reformers found its apologetic tone and its fictions indefensible.
narrative_structure: A four-part systematic exposition ordered by the analytical divisions of the law, each volume a continuous argument from history to institution to remedy.
meter_and_prosody: Elevated,periodic expository prose deliberately written for gentlemen as well as lawyers, with set-piece characterizations of the constitution and frequent literary allusion.
historical_context: Published by Clarendon Press at Oxford and W. Strahan in London between 1765 and 1769 after the lectures of the 1750s, it appeared in the age of Mansfield, of American rights rhetoric, and of Bentham's first Fragment; American lawyers before 1800 read it as a declaration of inherited liberty.
literary_significance: It fixed the vocabulary in which English and Americans spoke of law, liberty, and property; Bentham's attack on it founded philosophical radicalism, while its account of the balanced constitution entered the Federal Convention's debates.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Published at Oxford (Clarendon Press) and London in four volumes, 1765-69: volumes I and II in 1765 and 1766, volumes III and IV in 1768 and 1769; editions ran to a twelfth under Blackstone's lifetime (1783), and posthumous editions heavily altered his text; the first edition was long the basis of student facsimiles and of Wilfrid Prest's scholarly introduction to it.

title: An Analysis of the Laws of England
alternative_titles: Analysis of the Laws of England
description: Blackstone's elementary chart of the law, first printed in 1756 from his Oxford lectures and designed as a skeleton of heads and subdivisions by which a student might master the whole compass of the science. It distils the architecture that the Commentaries would later fill with narrative.
plot_or_argument: The Analysis divides the law into rights of persons and rights of things, private wrongs and public wrongs, and under each head lists the subordinate institutions in their logical order. Blackstone prefixes short historical remarks on the laws of the English before and after the conquest, and adds analytical tables that let the student see the law at a glance. The text assumes a reader of general cultivation, compressing doctrine into definitions and distinctions. Later editions, revised with the assistance of others, expanded the commentary around the skeleton.
narrative_structure: A tabular analysis: prefixed historical sketch, then four divisions resolved into numbered heads, with synoptical tables.
meter_and_prosody: Bare, condensed enumerative prose, maximally compressed definitions with minimal connectative tissue.
historical_context: Produced from the lectures Blackstone read as Vinerian student and tutor at Oxford, published in 1756 as a teaching aid and repeatedly reprinted with enlargements, it anticipates the architecture of the Commentaries and the century's mania for analyses and tables.
literary_significance: It became the standard mnemonic frame for legal study in England and America for decades, and a monument of the eighteenth century's faith that knowledge could be ordered in tables.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published Oxford, 1756; many editions followed, revised and enlarged under Blackstone's eye and after his death by other hands; reprinted in America as early as 1771.

title: Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Expectations
alternative_titles: Observations on Man
Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Expectations. Part I
description: David Hartley's associationist philosophy of the mind and religion, published in two parts in 1749: a 'Frame' deducing all mental life from vibration and association, and 'Duty and Expectations' grounding morality and revealed religion in that same mechanism. It became the foundation of the British associationist tradition.
plot_or_argument: Part I, on the Frame, proposes that outward objects produce vibrations in the sensory nerves and brain, which leave 'vibruncles', or permanent dispositions, the physical seats of memory and habit; from simple sensations the mind builds its whole world by association, so that tastes, motives, and even abstract ideas are compounded experiences. Part II argues that pleasures rise by association from the bodily to the moral and religious, that virtue is the attainment of the greatest happiness of the whole system of beings, and that providence's dispensations, including future punishment, are vindicated by their tendency to universal good. Hartley closes with a theodicy reading history and scripture as one curriculum of association toward eternal happiness.
narrative_structure: Two-part treatise: a physiological-metaphysical analysis of the Frame, followed by moral, religious, and eschatological applications.
meter_and_prosody: Uneven, intense, digressive prose of a thinker writing his scheme under pressure, with numbered propositions and long self-interrupting parentheses.
historical_context: Long maturing from the 1730s among the Hartley Circle and the Cambridge moralists' disputes, published in 1749 and noticed chiefly in the periodical reviews of the 1750s; its medical and Newtonian vocabulary places it between the New Science and the evangelical revival.
literary_significance: It founded the associationist psychology that Priestley, Darwin, and Mill inherited, gave the century its most influential account of the mechanism of taste and moral feeling, and shaped evangelical theories of character and atonement.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1749, in two parts; reprinted in 1755 with Priestley's Memoir of the author, and many times thereafter; the modern scholarly reprint is the facsimile editions of the 1960s-70s with introductions.

title: An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision
alternative_titles: A New Theory of Vision
description: Berkeley's first philosophical essay, arguing that distance and magnitude are not perceived by sight itself but learned by experience through association with touch and the straining of the eyes. It rewrote the geometry-based optics of the Cartesians and became a foundation stone of empiricist psychology of perception.
plot_or_argument: Berkeley shows that the immediate objects of sight are colours and figures with no necessary connexion to distance, and that distance is perceived only because certain visible ideas suggest ideas belonging originally to touch. He denies that the eye judges distance by lines, angles, or refractions known to the mind, and reinterprets Molyneux's problem of the cube and the globe: a person born blind, on receiving sight, would not identify by vision alone what he knew by touch. Apparent magnitude and the perception of situation follow from the same associative mechanism, and visual experience is shown to work like a language of signs. The essay closes by making vision a universal grammar divinely instituted, not a school of geometry.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in numbered sections, each proposition built on the previous analysis of the immediate objects of sight.
meter_and_prosody: Sparse, exact, demonstrative prose of short numbered paragraphs, the style of an experimental natural philosopher turned psychologist.
historical_context: Published in 1709 out of Berkeley's Dublin debates on the geometry of vision and framed by the new optics after Newton's Opticks of 1704; William Molyneux's question about distance perception gave it its shape.
literary_significance: It founded the science of perception on association rather than geometry, influenced Hume, Reid, and the empiricist tradition of psychology, and fed the eighteenth-century idea of nature as a language of signs.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1709; the Farther Thoughts on Vision was appended in later collections; the standard text is A. A. Luce and T. E. Jessup's edition of the Works (1948-57).

title: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
alternative_titles: The Principles of Human Knowledge
Principles of Human Knowledge
description: Berkeley's immaterialism laid out as a plain appeal to common sense: to be is to be perceived or to perceive, so that material substance is an absurdity, the external world is a system of ideas caused in us by God, and the scepticism the Cartesians feared is abolished. The Preface attacks abstract ideas and the main text runs through the consequences for science, mathematics, and religion.
plot_or_argument: Berkeley first denies that minds can frame truly abstract general ideas in the Lockeian sense, then argues that the very notion of unperceived matter is contradictory: the table, the moon, are nothing but sensible ideas, and ideas exist only in perceiving minds. Objects continue to exist when unperceived by us because some eternal mind perceives them, and the order, coherence, and steadiness of our ideas display the goodness and power of that spirit. Nature is accordingly a divine language or visual dial by which God instructs us, not an operation of dead matter and occult qualities; the atheist's material substratum vanishes, scepticism is cured, and the sciences are redeemed as rules for connecting experience rather than pictures of ultimates.
narrative_structure: Preface against abstract ideas, then a continuous numbered exposition of the thesis, with objections answered in short retorts, ending in religious and scientific application.
meter_and_prosody: Terse, aphoristic numbered prose of rhetorical directness, full of searching questions and dialogue compressed into monologue.
historical_context: Published in 1710 amid the after-effects of Locke's Essay and the freethinking assault on reason and religion; Berkeley issued it as a cheap pamphlet addressed to the common reader, and reissued it much enlarged in 1734.
literary_significance: It is the classic statement of idealist empiricism, the standing rival to Locke's representationalism, and the provocation around which the century's theories of mind, perception, and causation arranged themselves.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1710 (for J. Pepyat); second edition, much enlarged, 1734; collected in his Works, 1758; the standard text is Luce and Jessup's edition (1948-57).

title: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
alternative_titles: Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Three Parts
description: Berkeley's immaterialism restated in dialogue form, his most readable and most-quoted philosophical performance. Over three consecutive conversations on a walk, the sceptical materialist Hylas is led to concede that matter is unintelligible and that only spirits and their ideas exist, to the vindication of common sense and religion.
plot_or_argument: In the first dialogue Philonous drives Hylas from the dispute about secondary qualities to the concession that no sensible thing can exist unperceived. In the second, the doctrines of absolute space, time, and motion, and of matter as an inert occasion or unknown cause of ideas, are dismantled, and the real is redefined as what is perceived by minds. The third dialogue answers the charge that immaterialism breeds scepticism, solipsism, and atheism: the stability of things is secured by the divine perception, the senses give real knowledge of a world, and God is nearer to us than matter ever was. Hylas ends convinced, Philonous having shown that the paradox destroys only a philosophical fiction and leaves the garden, the table, and the body exactly as they were.
narrative_structure: Three consecutive dialogues framed by a brief narrative introduction of the speakers and their walk, rising from sensation to substance to theology.
principal_characters: Hylas; Philonous
meter_and_prosody: Lucid dramatic prose of question and retort, with the courtesy, warmth, and scene-painting of the Platonizing dialogue tradition.
historical_context: Published in London in 1713 as a popular companion and corrective to the difficult Treatise of 1710, after the furor over the Principles had made Berkeley a marked man in Dublin and London intellectual society.
literary_significance: It supplied the century's model of dialogue as philosophical argument and remains the standard entry to immaterialism; its Hylas-Philonous exchange shaped later philosophical dialogues from Hume to the Victorians.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1713; reprinted with the collected Works, 1758; the standard text is A. A. Luce and T. E. Jessup's edition of the Works (1948-57).

title: The Analyst
alternative_titles: The Analyst; or, A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician
The Analyst: or, A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician
description: Berkeley's attack on the foundations of the calculus, aimed at the mathematicians who scoff at the mysteries of religion while accepting infinitesimals and vanishing quantities on faith. It mocks the method of fluxions as 'the ghosts of departed quantities' and presses the analogy between mathematical and divine evidence.
plot_or_argument: Berkeley reviews the algebraists' methods for drawing tangents, quadratures, and cubical determinations, and shows that their mysterious infinitesimal differences and vanishing increments cannot be rigorously explained on their own terms. He distinguishes the sound practical rules from the defective logic of the fluxionary foundations, and charges that mathematicians conceal incoherence under jargon. Since nothing in this world can be understood without faith, he argues that the infidel who cannot believe in the arithmetic of infinities has no standing to deride the Trinity. The discourse ends with the famous query whether mathematical evidence is a better or a worse pattern for religious evidence than the sceptic admits.
narrative_structure: A single polemical discourse, expository first on the mathematicians' procedures, then critical, then theologically applicative.
meter_and_prosody: Sardonic, colloquial argumentative prose, the manner of a plain gentleman putting questions to specialists, with technical terms treated as so much mystic jargon.
historical_context: Published in 1731 when Berkeley was engaged in his Alciphron campaign against the freethinkers and when the Newtonian calculus was the standard weapon of deistic rationalists like Collins and Morgan; it provoked James Jurin's Reply and a decade of mathematical pamphlets, and eventually guided the foundations debate that reached Maclaurin and beyond.
literary_significance: It exposed genuine foundational weaknesses in the early calculus, helped drive eighteenth-century rigour, and became a classic of the analogy between mathematical and religious evidence; 'ghosts of departed quantities' entered the language.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1731; a second edition in 1734 with a reply to his critics; it provoked James Jurin's Plan of a Mathematical Demonstration (1734) and years of pamphlets; the standard text is Luce and Jessup's edition of the Works (1948-57).

title: Alciphron
alternative_titles: Alciphron, or the Minute Philosopher
description: Berkeley's dialogue against the freethinkers of his own day, figured as the ancient minute philosopher Alciphron, whose scepticism about religion, morality, and providence is answered not by metaphysics but by the visible evidence of Christianity's civilizing power. Its defence of the church as an historical and moral phenomenon was Berkeley's most publicistic work.
plot_or_argument: The dialogue opens on the minute philosopher Alciphron rejecting religion as enthusiasm and priestcraft, until the older Euphranor promises to prove Christianity by facts any candid critic must weigh. They examine the evidence of the founder's miracles and the prophecy of the church's enduring spread, arguing that a scheme which has tamed nations, fixed morals, and produced learning and charity cannot rest on a known imposture. Alciphron's scepticism about providence is met with the analogy of a well-governed state whose end exceeds present view. The closing dialogues answer the charge that Christianity has been the spoil of priests, showing it instead the patron of civil liberty and national union.
narrative_structure: Four consecutive dialogues, each answering one branch of the minute-philosopher's assault: miracles and evidence, prophecy and the church's spread, providence, and priestcraft and civilizing power.
principal_characters: Euphranor; Alciphron; Lysicles; Hippias; Cleontes
meter_and_prosody: Measured, courteous dialogic prose, more expansive than the Hylas dialogues, with set-piece historical argumentation.
historical_context: Published in 1732 in the immediate wake of the deist flush of Tindal and Collins and of the Shaftesburian reign of ridicule, and as Berkeley returned from his failed American college project; its portraits of the minute philosopher and of Lysicles were read as sketches of the freethinking club wits of the day.
literary_significance: It became the classic apologetic of evidential Christian moral history, influential in America and reprinted for debates at Harvard and Yale, and it is the century's fullest dialogue answer to freethinking ridicule.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1732; Berkeley issued a further edition with additions in 1734; reprinted in the Works; standard text Luce and Jessup (1948-57).

title: Siris
alternative_titles: Siris: A Chain of Philosophical Inquiries and Speculations concerning the Virtue of Tar-water
Siris: or, the Chain of Philosophy
description: Berkeley's strange and late 'chain of philosophical inquiry', occasioned by the vogue of tar-water as a medicine, which rises from remedies and agriculture through electricity, the animal fibre, and the Platonic one to a hymn to light and the divine mind. It is his most explicitly Platonizing and most idiosyncratic published work.
plot_or_argument: Berkeley praises tar-water as a specific for many distempers and derives from its humble origin a chain of enquiry into virtue in physical things, fire, air, and electricity as the universal active medium. He speculates that a far subtler electric or aetherial spirit pervades and quickens nature, the seat of vital motion and of the animal spirits, and that light is the most universal being whose finite emanation binds the world. From physics the chain ascends to Platonic ontology: the one, the good, and intellectual light, closing with an apostrophe to the source of light and truth. The book thus makes medicine the stairway to natural theology.
narrative_structure: A serial chain of short linked enquiries, each section drawing the previous upward, in the manner of a Platonizing rhapsody.
meter_and_prosody: A rising, sometimes rapturous prose of questions and responsive speculations, with a long hymnic peroration in rhythmic periods.
historical_context: Published in 1744 after Berkeley's return from America and the failure of his Bermuda college scheme, in the season of electrical excitement following Franklin and of popular medical specifics; it was reviewed, mocked, and translated on the continent.
literary_significance: It stands as the century's most curious fusion of empiricist science and Platonist mysticism, and it renewed the ancient doctrine of the one and of vital spirit in a modern scientific vocabulary.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London and Dublin, 1744; rapidly followed by a second edition and a Latin translation; the standard text is Luce and Jessup's edition of the Works (1948-57).

title: An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue
alternative_titles: An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue, in Two Treatises
Concerning Beauty and Virtue
description: Hutcheson's two-treatise defence of the moral sense and the sense of beauty against Hobbes and Mandeville, arguing that the determinations of taste and virtue are immediate, disinterested senses of the human frame. It gave the Scottish Enlightenment its founding vocabulary of benevolence and moral sense.
plot_or_argument: The first treatise shows that beauty and deformity are perceived at once by an internal sense, not by calculation of advantage, and that the harmony of parts, novelty, and the intellectual beauties of science and art obey the same sense. The second treatise argues that virtue is loved for benevolence, the quality of intending happiness to others, against the egoism that resolves all affection into self-love; the moral sense approves disinterested affection immediately. Calculations of utility, Hutcheson insists, follow rather than found our approvals, and the pleasure of virtue is proportioned to the extent of its benevolence. A concluding mathematical language of morals attempts to express praise as benevolence multiplied by the number possessed.
narrative_structure: Two linked treatises on beauty and virtue, each an analytic demonstration with objections answered, plus a closing section proposing a calculus of morals.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, modest, scholastic-plain prose of a teacher's lecture-room, with numbered distinctions and the famous arithmetic notation of moral worth.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1725 as Hutcheson had begun his Glasgow lectureship amid the row over his appointment; the third edition of 1729 was greatly enlarged. The Inquiry answered Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and the rationalist ethics of Clarke and Wollaston within the debate Shaftesbury had opened.
literary_significance: It fixed the moral-sense scheme, taught the century to speak of benevolence as the essence of virtue, and directly shaped Hume, the American founders' idea of the pursuit of happiness, and the whole sentimentalist tradition.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1725; second edition 1726; third edition, much enlarged with the arithmetic of morals and further additions, 1729; reprinted frequently and translated into several languages; standard scholarly edition by Wolfgang Leiser (2007).

title: An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
alternative_titles: Essay on the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
description: Hutcheson's anatomy of the affections, mapping calm and violent passions, theocentric and sympathetic affections, and the pleasures they bring, and appending the Illustrations on the Moral Sense against Clarke, Wollaston, and Mandeville. It is the sentimentalist psychology that underwrote his ethics.
plot_or_argument: The Essay classifies the affections into calm and violent, self-, other-, and God-directed, and shows that our happiness depends on the temper of the heart rather than its outward objects. Benevolence yields the sweetest, most steady enjoyments; malice, envy, and excessive self-love torment themselves, while the approbation of the moral sense attends every generous affection. The Illustrations then attack the rationalist moralists for mistaking cool self-interest for virtue and for making utility the measure of moral good, showing by examples that we approve disinterested benevolence immediately and independently of interest. The instruction of the passions by habit and the place of the moral sense in education conclude the argument.
narrative_structure: Two paired parts: a systematic essay on the affections and a group of Illustrations conducted as critical essays against named opponents.
meter_and_prosody: Warm, exemplum-rich prose of the preacher-philosopher, long in sympathetic description and sharp in polemic rejoinder.
historical_context: Published in 1728 after the Inquiry and amid Hutcheson's Glasgow disputes with the rationalist school; the Illustrations take up the cause of Shaftesbury's sentimentalism against the moral philosophy of the English rationalists and of Mandeville.
literary_significance: Its psychology of the passions became the standard sentimentalist textbook, training Hume, Adam Smith, and the preachers in the moral cultivation of the affections and the priority of benevolence.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London and Dublin, 1728? safer: published 1728; reprinted 1735 and 1746, and translated into French; often bound with later editions of the Inquiry.

title: A Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy
alternative_titles: Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy, in Three Books
Moral Philosophy (Hutcheson)
description: Hutcheson's mature summary of his ethical system in three books, written as a student vade mecum: the moral sense and its determinations, self-love and benevolence in their due proportions, and the obligations of the natural, social, and divine life. Its final maxim made the greatest happiness of the greatest numbers the sole rule of duty.
plot_or_argument: Book I grounds virtue in the moral sense, showing that this sense determines us to approve benevolent affections and that the laws of nature are intelligible only through it. Book II analyses self-love and its vanity when made the end, and benevolence as the happiness of the agent as well as of the species. Book III deduces the duties to God, to ourselves, and to our neighbours from the dictates of right reason joined to benevolence, and closes on the famous formula that the action is best which procures the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers. The whole is compressed into aphoristic numbered sections for classroom use.
narrative_structure: Three books of numbered propositions in catechetic order, each doctrine placed under its heads and their moral.
meter_and_prosody: Bare, sententious, heavily numbered textbook prose, almost a series of theses, with occasional passages of the older warmth.
historical_context: Published in 1747, distilling Hutcheson's forty years of Glasgow teaching into a classroom manual read by the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and by students at Harvard and Princeton.
literary_significance: It transmitted utilitarian's first canonical formula and the moral-sense system to the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and the American founding, becoming the most-copied ethics textbook of the colonies.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1747; reprinted many times, translated into French and German, and used at Harvard and Princeton; the standard scholarly edition is Aaron Garrett's (Indianapolis, 2002).

title: A Treatise of Human Nature
alternative_titles: Treatise of Human Nature
A Treatise of Human Nature: Being an Attempt to Introduce the Experimental Method of Reasoning into Moral Subjects
description: Hume's first and most ambitious work, an attempt to rebuild philosophy on the experimental method by tracing all of human understanding, the passions, and morals to their principles in experience. Books I and II appeared in 1739 and Book III in 1740, and the Treatise became the foundation of empiricist philosophy, sceptical naturalism, and the science of human nature.
plot_or_argument: Book I derives every simple idea from a preceding impression, then dismantles the fictions of substance, causation as necessary connection, and the identity of the self, showing that custom, not reason, is the guide of life; the famous conclusion admits the sceptic's demonstrations against probability while restoring nature's authority over them. Book II classifies the passions into direct and indirect, explains sympathy as the mechanism by which we receive the feelings of others, and analyses the will, liberty, and necessity. Book III founds morals on sentiment, argues that reason is and ought only the slave of the passions, derives justice and fidelity from artificial conventions grown useful, and closes with the catalogue of the natural and artificial virtues. The whole rests on the psychological claim that the mind's operations, like the body's, obey discoverable regular laws.
narrative_structure: Three books in progressive architecture, understanding then passions then morals, each subdivided into parts and sections, with a closing book-section and an Advertisement of the Enquiry plan.
meter_and_prosody: Precise, animated, exemplum-driven expository prose, its sceptical passages rising to meditative periodic grandeur, the style of the moral philosopher as man of letters.
historical_context: Written mostly at La Fleche in France, published anonymously in Edinburgh and London in 1739-40, and received, in Hume's own later phrase, as still-born from the press; it answered Locke, Berkeley, Butler, Clarke, and Mandeville while founding the new science of human nature.
literary_significance: It is the masterwork of the Scottish Enlightenment and one of the two or three greatest works of English-language philosophy, source of the induction and causation problems, the is-ought distinction, the bundle theory of self, and sentimentalist ethics.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; Hume acknowledged it in My Own Life and the Advertisements.
bibliographical_notes: Books I and II published Edinburgh and London, 1739; Book III 1740; the Advertisement subjoined to Book III foreshadowed the Enquiries; the standard scholarly edition is David Fate Norton and Mary Norton's Oxford edition (2000-09).

title: Essays Moral and Political
alternative_titles: Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary (1741-42 volumes)
Essays Moral and Political, Vol. I
description: Hume's first popular publications, two volumes of essays (1741-42) on taste, passion, the stoics, the jealousy of trade, party, and the balance of power, which established his literary reputation where the Treatise had failed. They introduced the essay as an instrument of the new psychology of refinement and modern politics.
plot_or_argument: The moral essays argue that refinement of the age softens the man rather than enervates him, that a true delicacy of taste depends on a sound sense joined to passion, and that the ancient stoic ideal of extirpating the passions is an enthusiastic self-deception; the modern essayist counsels the regulation rather than the destruction of feeling. The political essays analyse the vices of party, the jealousy of trade as a groundless zero-sum fear, the blessings of industry, civility, and refinements, and the delicate balance of authority and liberty in a modern commonwealth. Essays on the first principles of government ground political obligation in convention and utility rather than an original contract. Together they sketch the 'taste and temperament' of commercial modernity the later writings would theorize.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of independent essays in two volumes, ordered moral then political and historical, with no sustained argument across papers.
meter_and_prosody: The clear, balanced middle style of the polite essay, periodic where meditative, pointed where polemical, with its signature generalizations in short declaratives.
historical_context: Volume I appeared in Edinburgh in 1741 and Volume II in 1742, during Hume's failed embassy and clergymen's uproar over the Treatise, and after the pattern of the Spectator papers was already worn; Hume's essays reinvented the form as moral philosophy in undress.
literary_significance: They made Hume a man of letters before he was a philosopher, fixed the classic essays on taste and the jealousy of trade, and supplied the humane public philosophy that the Enquiries and History later carried.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Vol. I Edinburgh, 1741; Vol. II Edinburgh and London, 1742; reprinted and amalgamated into the Essays and Treatises on Several Subjects from 1748; the standard edition is Eugene Miller's Essays Moral, Political, and Literary (1985; rev. 1987).

title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
alternative_titles: Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding
description: Hume's reconstruction of the first part of the Treatise as a polished Enquiry, recast when it appeared as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding and retitled in 1750. It is the classic statement of the problem of induction, the analysis of causation, and the sceptical discussions of miracles and of the arguments for providence.
plot_or_argument: Hume divides all objects of the mind into impressions and ideas, fixes the copy principle, and finds in custom the answer to how experience reaches beyond what is immediately present: our reasonings concerning matters of fact are founded not on demonstration but on habit. Causation is then analysed as constant conjunction with a felt determination of the mind, and necessary connection is projected onto nature. The sections on liberty and necessity reconcile the will with determinism by redefining freedom as a power of acting according to the will's determination, and the celebrated section on miracles argues that no testimony can amount to proof of a miracle unless its falshood would be more miraculous than the fact, while the discussion of design demurs that an order in nature argues only to an artisan's artifice, not to a benevolent Providence.
