The book ends by committing the school metaphysics to the flames.
narrative_structure: Twelve successive enquiries, each isolating and enlarging one chapter of the Treatise's argument, the later sections turning to liberty, miracles, and natural religion.
meter_and_prosody: Supple, lucid, often epigrammatic prose of deliberate literary polish, with famous rhetorical closers on the metaphysicians and on miracle testimony.
historical_context: Published at London in 1748 in the wake of Butler's Analogy and the Woolston controversy over miracles and evidence, after Hume's failed candidacy for the Edinburgh chair; it recast his earlier metaphysics for the general reader.
literary_significance: It is the most influential text in the empiricist tradition, source of the induction and causation problems in their standard modern form, and the founding document of the philosophical discussion of miracle testimony and natural theology.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1748 as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding; reissued 1750 under its familiar title; the last edition revised by Hume appeared in 1777; the standard scholarly text is the Nidditch Oxford edition of the two Enquiries.

title: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
alternative_titles: Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
description: Hume's recasting of Treatise Book III, the mature sentimentalist ethics, and in his own judgment incomparably the best of his writings. It argues that moral distinctions arise from a sentiment of approbation attentive to utility and agreeableness, and re-reads the catalogue of the virtues as a catalogue of their value to life.
plot_or_argument: Hume first shows that our moral sentiments respond to characters as a whole and not to single acts, and that utility, public or private, is a principal source of the esteem we pay to benevolence, justice, fidelity, and honour. He confutes the rationalist and egoist systems by exhibiting the calm general sentiment, the moral taste, which makes virtue lovely and vice odious independently of self-interest, and explains the artificial virtues of justice and allegiance by the evident usefulness of their general systems. A celebrated appendix attacks the monkish virtues of self-denial and humility as enervating and useless to society, and the closing section asks whether morality be founded on reason or sentiment, answering in favour of sentiment. The whole is written as a cheerful vindication of virtue as the charm and benefit of life.
narrative_structure: Nine sections progressing from the origin of moral distinction through utility, benevolence, and justice to the reason-versus-sentiment dispute, with three appended sections.
meter_and_prosody: Hume's most generous and polished prose, ironic and rhetorically enriched, with sententious closes and an extended set-piece against the monkish virtues.
historical_context: Published in 1751 against the Glasgow debates with the rationalist moral school and the critical neglect of the Treatise; its appendix on the monkish virtues made its anti-austerian temper unmistakable to every reader.
literary_significance: It is the classic document of sentimentalist ethics and one of the sources of utilitarian moral theory, decisive for Adam Smith, the classical utilitarians, and the later virtue tradition.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1751, for A. Millar; reprinted in the Essays and Treatises on Several Subjects and the collected editions; the standard scholarly text is the Nidditch Oxford edition of the two Enquiries.

title: Political Discourses
alternative_titles: Fourteen Political Discourses
description: Hume's essays on money, trade, credit, population, and the sinews of public power, published in London in 1752 and instantly the most discussed economic writing of the decade. They argued that commercial growth is self-sustaining, that the balance of trade doctrines are sophistry, and that public credit is the Achilles heel of modern states.
plot_or_argument: The discourses trace how industry, knowledge, and refinement spread from a cultivated court and city to the whole state, so that trade, not hoarded bullion, constitutes a nation's real opulence. Hume demolishes the jealousy of trade and mercantilist balances, shows money to be a veil over labour, and works out the price-specie-flow logic by which trade surpluses self-correct through rising prices. He then analyses interest as the price of the scarcity of lent capital, taxes, credit, paper money, colonies, and population, closing with gloomy reflections on the perpetual tendency of public credit to subvert modern government. The political discourses on the parties of antiquity and of England and on the limits of human policy frame the whole.
narrative_structure: Fourteen connected discourses in a loose sequence from growth and trade to money, interest, credit, taxes, and the balance of parties.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, rapid argumentative prose of the practised essayist, with numbers used as rhetoric and abrupt generalizing closers.
historical_context: Published in 1752 amid the decade's debates over paper credit, population, and the balance of trade; its opening discourse grew out of Hume's celebrated statistical controversy with the Chevalier d'Eon over the comparative greatness of France and England.
literary_significance: It was Adam Smith's declared predecessor in commercial theory and one of the most reprinted, translated, and quoted economic texts of the century, the bridge from the mercantilists to classical political economy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1752, for A. Millar; reprinted within the Essays and Treatises on Several Subjects from 1754; the standard scholarly edition is Duncan Forbes's Cambridge Selected Essays (1993), and the discourses were translated into French by the abbe de la Chapelle in 1754.

title: The Natural History of Religion
alternative_titles: Of the Natural History of Religion
description: Hume's account of how polytheism arose from human fears and hopes and how the human mind tends, through adulation and complaint, back toward a single supreme being: religion explained as a natural history of the mind rather than a truth discovered. First printed among the Four Dissertations of 1757 and composed by 1751-52.
plot_or_argument: Hume argues that the first ideas of the Deity arose not from contemplation of nature's order but from the anxiety and hopes of ordinary life, which clothed unknown causes with human shapes and interests. Because the motives of polytheism are the ordinary interests of men, its gods are limited, sociable, and ludicrous, and its rituals familiar; monotheism, by contrast, lifts God above human comprehension and so inflames priests and fanatics into a jealousy of divine attribute. Polytheism thus proves more gentle and more favourable to civil liberty, while the road from polytheism to monotheism runs through flattery, and the return to superstition through philosophy is via enthusiasm and the pretended reason of natural theology. The closing pages make the whole history of religion a lesson in the uniform passions of the human species.
narrative_structure: A single dissertation in twenty-eight short sections, moving from origins in fear through polytheism's domestic character to monotheism, superstition, and enthusiasm.
meter_and_prosody: Ironically courteous expository prose, cool generalizations about 'the religious' set against the heated vocabulary of the priesthoods, with a famous dry closing cadence.
historical_context: Conceived in the early 1750s, published in London in 1757 in the volume of Four Dissertations that also contained the Dissertation on the Passions and the two historical dissertations, in the season of the French and Indian War's zealotries and of the Church-of England controversy over enthusiasm.
literary_significance: It founded the natural history and psychological explanation of religion, the ancestor of the scientific study of religion from Spencer to contemporary cognitive accounts of religion, and the most quoted religious writing of the Enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1757, within Four Dissertations, the volume that also contained the Dissertation on the Passions; extracted by Hume into the collected Essays and Treatises and reprinted independently throughout the century.

title: The History of England
alternative_titles: History of England, from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688
Hume's History of England
description: Hume's six-volume history of England, written backwards from the Stuarts to Caesar and the earliest ages, and the most widely read history of the century. It narrates the growth of the constitution, party, and commerce from a philosophical standpoint hostile alike to Whig martyr legends and Tory divine-right tales.
plot_or_argument: The Stuart volumes first show the fatal collision between the prerogative and the commons, the errors of Charles I and of his opponents, and the way enthusiasm and faction made civil war and then commonwealth plausible; the Tudor volumes trace the centralizing monarchy, the reformation, and the rise of the people's claims; the early volumes from the invasion of Caesar through the Plantagenets and the establishment of the commons narrate how law, property, and civility emerged slowly out of conquest, feudal anarchy, and monastic learning. Throughout, Hume explains events by the opposition of authority and liberty, the interests of ranks, and the unnoticed moral effects of commerce and the laws, refusing providential and party readings alike. The volume covering the accession of the house of Stuart to the revolution of 1688 closes his own published series.
narrative_structure: Six volumes issued in reverse chronological order between 1754 and 1762, each a continuous political narrative with inserted constitutional, legal, and economic remarks.
principal_characters: Henry VIII; Elizabeth I; Mary Queen of Scots; James I; Charles I; Cromwell; William III
meter_and_prosody: The level, capacious, periodic historiographic prose of the philosophical historian, marked by balanced judgment clauses and sardonic character portraits.
historical_context: Written while Hume was librarian of the Faculty of Advocates in Edinburgh and supported by copies of records from London, the History drew furious party reviews and episcopal remonstrance, yet made Hume financially independent and a European name.
literary_significance: It was the standard English history for half a century, shaped nineteenth-century historiography and the Whig-Tory synthesis, and is still studied as the monument of history written as the science of human nature applied.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Volumes on the Stuarts appeared 1754-57, the Tudor volume 1759, and the early British histories to the revolution of 1688 through 1762; it became the textbook of the English-speaking historical reading public; a modern scholarly selection is Duncan Forbes's History of England: From the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688 (1975).

title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
description: Hume's posthumous dialogue on natural theology, held between Cleanthes the empiricist design-theorist, Demea the sceptical orthodox, and Philo the ironic destructor of the argument from design. Left in manuscript at his death and published in 1779 by his friends at his request, it is the most famous English statement of the problem of natural religion.
plot_or_argument: Cleanthes proposes the argument from design as an a posteriori analogy: the order of the world proves an intelligent cause proportioned to its effects. Philo, by turns playful and devastating, presses the weaknesses of the analogy: design is but one hypothesis among many, the world may be a crude embryo of a better system, an imperfect author, or the work of a plurality of gods, and from the mixture of good and ill in nature no perfection of the cause can be inferred. Demea then argues from the misery and vanity of human life toward a mystical, unknowable deity, which Philo's closing sceptical piety hardly distinguishes from atheism. The dialogue ends on the question whether the true religion can be defended by human reason at all, without resolving it.
narrative_structure: Twelve parts of continuous dialogue in the classical manner, the argument rising through analogy, scepticism, and theodicy to an unresolved conclusion.
principal_characters: Cleanthes; Demea; Philo
meter_and_prosody: Measured dialogic prose of courtesy and retort in the classical manner, Philo's demolitions shaded beneath urbane periods and long rhetorical cadences.
historical_context: Composed in fragments from the early 1750s and revised through the 1770s, it was withheld in Hume's lifetime and published posthumously in 1779 at his written desire, amid the public controversy over his dying scepticism reported by Boswell and others.
literary_significance: It remains the standard literary and philosophical presentation of the design argument and its critics, a touchstone for the philosophy of religion from nineteenth-century editions to contemporary debates.
attribution_notes: Published posthumously under Hume's direction; the date and extent of composition (1750-1776) are matters of scholarly inference from manuscripts and letters.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1779, with a prefatory advertisement explaining the posthumous occasion; reprinted constantly through the nineteenth century, often with editorial notes; Hume's own request that publication wait until after his death is recorded in his letters and in My Own Life.

title: My Own Life
alternative_titles: The Life of David Hume (1777 autobiographical sketch)
description: Hume's short, serene autobiography, written in April 1776 and read to the club in Edinburgh in that year; published in 1777 as the preface to the fourth volume of the edition of his works. It became one of the most quoted self-characters in English, a model of the philosophic autobiography of a mind surveying its own impartiality.
plot_or_argument: Hume recounts his birth and family, his studious childhood, the writing of the Treatise in France, its being still-born from the press, and the gradual success of the Essays, the Political Discourses, and above all the History of England. He tells of his Edinburgh offices, the embassy in France, and the quarrel with Rousseau, which he narrates as a notable incident of the malady of self-love in a mind he pitied rather than resented. His return to Scotland produced the Natural History of Religion, the Dialogues, and the revised editions of his works. He sums up his character as mild, candid, cheerful, and sociable, a lover of pleasure more than of ambition, and closes on his own philosophy in the face of death without hope of a future life.
narrative_structure: A continuous compact autobiography in short paragraphs, chronological from birth to the year of writing.
principal_characters: David Hume as narrator and subject
meter_and_prosody: The clearest, coolest middle prose, self-portraiture in declaratives, every judgment of others balanced by an appeal to the testimony of enemies and friends.
historical_context: Written in the spring of 1776 as Hume faced the cancer that killed him in August, it was intended to control the story of his life and death against Boswell's evangelizing and the churchmen's scandal over his dying composure.
literary_significance: A founding document of the secular autobiography and of the Enlightenment's self-image of the philosophic mind, constantly quoted for its account of the still-born Treatise and its closing serenity.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Written in April 1776 and read to the Select Society in Edinburgh; published in 1777 as the preface to the last volume of the four-volume edition of his Works; standard printings attach it to selections of Hume's letters and to the deathbed controversy.

title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
alternative_titles: Theory of Moral Sentiments
description: Adam Smith's first great work, the fullest elaboration of the moral-sense tradition through the mechanism of sympathy and the impartial spectator. It explains how fellow-feeling, admiration, and the desire for praiseworthiness generate moral judgment, duty, and virtue, and it remains the century's most comprehensive treatise on the social psychology of ethics.
plot_or_argument: Part I shows that we judge the propriety of another's feelings by imagining ourselves in his situation, sympathy being the imaginary transposition of spectator and agent, and that the senses of propriety and justice arise from this exchange of perspectives. Part II traces the feelings of merit and demerit, the rules of justice and beneficence, and the influence of custom and fashion on moral sentiment. Part III introduces the impartial spectator as the internal judge and the desire for praiseworthiness as the mature moral motive. Parts IV and V analyse the corruption of the moral sentiments by the love of riches and rank, and survey the rival systems of ethics from the ancients to the moderns. Part VI completes the taxonomy of the virtues of prudence, justice, beneficence, and self-command. The whole grounds society not on contract but on the mutual mirror of sympathetic sentiments.
narrative_structure: Six parts of graduated argument, from the analysis of sympathy through the general rules and the impartial spectator to the history of ethical systems and the taxonomy of the virtues.
meter_and_prosody: An expansive, illustrative lecture prose dense with social observation, its famous generalizations stated in balanced declaratives, addressed alike to polite and philosophical readers.
historical_context: Grown from Smith's Glasgow lectures begun in the early 1750s and published in London in 1759 with Hume's encouragement, it appeared in the season of the Edinburgh and Glasgow debates on scepticism and the French materialists and was revised by Smith through five later editions.
literary_significance: It supplied the moral psychology for commercial society's self-understanding, is the necessary companion to the Wealth of Nations, and anchors the modern revival of sympathy-based ethics and the study of the Scottish Enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1759, for A. Millar and T. Cadell; revised through several editions, the final sixth appearing in 1790 with large additions; the standard critical text is D. D. Raphael and A. L. Macfie's edition (Oxford, 1976) in the Glasgow edition of Smith's Works.

title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
alternative_titles: The Wealth of Nations
description: Adam Smith's founding book of political economy, an inquiry into how the wealth of nations grows through the division of labour, free mutual exchange, and the accumulation of stock, and why monopoly, mercantilist regulation, and colonial exclusive trade obstruct that growth. Published in two volumes in London in 1776, it reframed the science of society's material life.
plot_or_argument: Book I derives the division of labour from the propensity to truck and barter, limits it by the extent of the market, and resolves the price of commodities into wages, profit, and rent, with the famous observation that the butcher, brewer, and baker serve us from self-love rather than benevolence. Book II classifies stock, capital, and money, and distinguishes productive from unproductive labour as the real determinant of national accumulation. Book III narrates the history of European development from the fall of Rome: the rise of towns, the slow victory of urban manufactures over rural dependence, and the commerce that introduced order and personal liberty. Book IV dismantles the mercantile system, the restraints on import, and the project of colonial monopoly, with the East India company among its indicted villains, and Book V grounds the necessary public works, institutions of education, and revenue of a civilized state. The whole makes commercial interdependence, not state power, the engine of national opulence.
narrative_structure: Five books moving from first principles of value and distribution through the real history of Europe to the polemic against the mercantile system and the policy of natural liberty.
meter_and_prosody: Long analytic prose of lecture-derived clarity, built on homely exemplars of pin-makers and corn-farmers, its argumentative climaxes in sustained ironic indictments of the interested systems of commerce and law.
historical_context: Written after Smith's tutorial tour abroad and years of Edinburgh and Glasgow teaching, amid the American crisis and the East India company's scandals, it was published in the year of the Declaration of Independence and read immediately across Europe and in Parliament.
literary_significance: It is the foundational text of classical political economy and of liberal thought about markets and empire, the book against and from which all later economics, from Ricardo and Marx to the present, has defined itself.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1776, in two volumes, for W. Strahan and T. Cadell; a fifth edition appeared in 1789; the standard critical text is the Glasgow edition (Oxford University Press, 1976) in the Works of Adam Smith.

title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense
alternative_titles: Inquiry into the Human Mind
description: Reid's founding statement of the philosophy of common sense, begun as a challenge to the way of ideas and first delivered as Glasgow lectures in the early 1760s. It argues that the faculties of perception, memory, and conception are original powers given by nature and trusted by every human being, and that scepticism is the inevitable harvest of treating the mind's natural testimony as a hypothesis.
plot_or_argument: Reid reviews the history of speculative philosophy and the essence of language as prefaces to a grammar of the human mind. He distinguishes sensation from perception and shows that perception of external objects is a natural and original judgment, not an inference from ideas or a calculus of signs. The chapters on the five senses demonstrate, against Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, that the mind is endowed with faculties whose deliverances carry their own authority; the same argument is run through memory, conception, and belief. The concluding chapters expose the ideal theory as scepticism's engine and defend the common judgments of mankind as first principles, the judge and party together in the cause of reason.
narrative_structure: Seven chapters of progressive anatomy of the faculties, each opening from common observation and closing against the theoretical philosophy, with prefatory chapters on language and the history of speculation.
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous, plain, hortatory prose of a preacher-philosopher, direct address, rhetorical questions, and blunt refusals of technical jargon.
historical_context: Published in 1764 with a dedication to the Glasgow physician who had pressed the lectures into print, after Reid's appointment to the Glasgow chair and amid the faculty's running controversy with Hume; it was answered, and answered again, through the following decade.
literary_significance: It founded the school of common-sense philosophy, reshaped the epistemology of perception, and is the central document of the Aberdeen and Glasgow resistance to sceptical empiricism, revived in modern philosophy of mind and epistemology.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1764, for A. Millar and T. Cadell, with Glasgow and Edinburgh booksellers; the standard scholarly text is Paul Wood's edition (Edinburgh, 2000) in the Reid series.

title: Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man
description: Reid's mature encyclopaedia of the mind, the Glasgow lectures of the 1770s? keep general: the mature summing-up of common-sense philosophy, eight essays on the powers of perception, memory, consciousness, conception, judgment, reasoning, and taste. It is the fullest statement of the anatomy of the human understanding after Locke and the companion to its successor volume on the active powers.
plot_or_argument: The first essays analyse the power of perception in its original and acquired forms, the perceptions that make a landscape readable to the eye, and the roles of memory and consciousness as the direct testimony of the mind. Conception, the conceptions of primary and secondary qualities, and the general conceptions by which language works, are then distinguished from the principles of judgment, the self-evident first principles of common sense which the sceptic must borrow before he can argue. The closing essays examine the power of reasoning and the province of taste and criticism. Throughout, Reid answers the sceptical account of belief and the geometry of probabilities, reasserting that the natural faculties are, and must be, the measure of their own trustworthiness.
narrative_structure: Eight essays in the manner of the Glasgow lectures, each on one intellectual power, arranged from perception through judgment to reasoning and criticism.
literary_form: philosophical essays on the mental powers
meter_and_prosody: The plain, cumulative, exemplum-rich prose of the lecture-room, with long definitions and numbered first principles delivered in a tone of candid remonstrance.
historical_context: Published in 1785 after years of Glasgow lectures and amid the running Scottish response to Hume and to Beattie's Essay on Truth, it preceded the companion volume on the active powers and was widely reviewed and soon translated on the continent.
literary_significance: It consolidated the school of common-sense philosophy into the century's great alternative account of the mind and remains the standard text of the non-sceptical Scottish epistemology that shaped the American common-sense tradition through Reid's Scottish pupils and their descendants.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1785 at Edinburgh and London; reprinted in the collected Works in the nineteenth century and many times since; the scholarly text is in the Edinburgh University Press critical editions of Reid's works.

title: An Essay on the History of Civil Society
alternative_titles: Essay on the History of Civil Society
description: Ferguson's philosophical history of society, the founding text of the Scottish stage theory of social development, tracing mankind from the hunter and shepherd through tillage, commerce, and polished policy. It warns that the very arts and refinements which advance civil society may enervate the citizens and endanger liberty, and it argued for a science of man attentive to unintended consequences.
plot_or_argument: Ferguson begins from human nature as active, ingenuous, and perfectible, a species whose history is the slow education of the race. He then traces the stages of society, the hunter's tent, the shepherd's camp, the tiller's village, and the commerce that peoples cities with arts, ranks, and laws, showing each institution to be the result of human action but not of a design to found it. Polished society brings the division of labour, the machinery of state, credit, and standing armies, and with them the danger that a people of traders will surrender public freedom to private ease. The essay closes on the contingency of history, the possibility of corruption even in republics, and a Stoic counsel that the species, like the individual, must earn its character through exertion.
narrative_structure: A continuous essay moving from the philosophy of human nature through the successive stages of society to the moral and political diagnosis of polished commercial life.
meter_and_prosody: Nervous, energetic, sententious prose full of rhetorical questions and republican apostrophes, alternating cool analysis with moral alarm.
historical_context: Composed after Ferguson succeeded Adam Smith in the Edinburgh chair of moral philosophy, the fruit of the lecture theatre and the Select Society circle, and published in 1767; it was translated into German and French within a decade.
literary_significance: It created the science of society's vocabulary of stages, unintended consequences, and civic humanism in a commercial age, standing between the civic republicanism of the ancients and the sociology of the nineteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh and London, 1767; revised and enlarged in several lifetime editions; modern scholarly editions include the Cambridge text edited by Duncan Forbes and Fania Oz-Salzberger's edition.

title: The History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
alternative_titles: The Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
description: Ferguson's narrative history of Rome from its agricultural and citizen origins through conquest, civil discord, and the loss of the republic, written by the philosopher of civil society as its practical case study. It showed how the virtues that built Rome, martial spirit and public ambition, dissolved the very constitution they had founded.
plot_or_argument: The history opens on the earliest ages, Rome's peasant militia, patrician families, and kingless commonwealth, and follows the struggle of the orders as the engine of Roman liberty. It narrates the progress of conquest, the agrarian laws, the rise of the commons and their leaders, the civil wars of Marius, Sylla, Pompey, and Caesar, and the final extinction of the republic under Augustus. Ferguson treats the dissolution not as a mere conspiracy of great men but as the structural outcome of empire without civic capacity, the corruption of the people, and the army's transfer of loyalty from the state to its generals, closing with reflections on the fate of free states.
narrative_structure: Four books of continuous narrative from the regal and early republican ages to the establishment of the monarchy under Augustus, with inserted institutional and moral reflections.
principal_characters: Romulus; the Gracchi; Marius; Sylla; Pompey; Caesar; Cicero; Augustus
meter_and_prosody: A declamatory, periodic prose in the manner of the classical historians, its judgment-sentences modelled on the moralities of republican rise and decline.
historical_context: Published in Edinburgh and London in 1769, a work of Edinburgh lecture culture and of the age's Roman republicanism, written in the same years as the Wilkes and parliamentary debates that made the fate of free states a live British subject.
literary_significance: It became the standard Scottish reading of Rome's fall as a lesson in the political sociology of liberty, much admired in its day and read by the founders of the American republic as a mirror of corrupt commonwealths.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1769 at Edinburgh and London; reprinted repeatedly, translated into French, and long issued with the Essay on the History of Civil Society.

title: Observations Concerning the Distinction of Ranks in Society
alternative_titles: The Distinction of Ranks
Observations Concerning the Distinction of Ranks in Society, Vol. I
description: John Millar's pioneering social history of ranks, gender, and law, the first full application of the Scottish theory of society to the changing relations of masters and servants, sexes, ages, and conditions. It argued that the manner of subsistence shapes the laws, manners, and domestic relations of a people.
plot_or_argument: Millar traces the distinctions of rank from the ranks of the savage and pastoral states, through the slavery and villeinage of agricultural societies, to the graded dependencies of commercial life. He shows the legal condition of servants, tenants, and slaves to vary with the species of industry and the balance of power between the rich and the state. A celebrated sequence treats the rank of the female sex in each stage, arguing that civilisation softens domestic authority and raises women's consideration, and other chapters follow the relations of parents and children, ages, and professions. The printed book, the fruit of the Glasgow lectures, ends unfinished in its design, its completed first volumes carrying the argument from dependence to the domestic and sexual orders of polished society.
narrative_structure: A continuous analytical history in successive chapters on each relation of rank, each stage compared across nations and epochs.
meter_and_prosody: Cool, comparative, case-rich prose of the jurisprudential lecturer, long historical illustrations drawn to a general law of social development.
historical_context: Published in 1771 from Millar's Glasgow lectures, in the decade of the stage-theory efflorescence and after Smith's and Ferguson's accounts of society; the volume carried only the designed first half, the remaining volumes issuing in the 1780s and 1790s from lectures revised against the French Revolution.
literary_significance: It founded the history of social ranks and of gender as a scholarly subject, supplied the stage-consciousness that ran into the nineteenth century through Comte and historical sociology, and remains a classic of Enlightenment thought about society and women.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1771, for T. Cadell; several eighteenth-century editions followed; the work is now read in facsimile, and the unfinished design is documented in Millar's lecture notes and the later volumes.

title: An Essay on Truth
alternative_titles: Essay on Truth
description: James Beattie's verbose, pugnacious vindication of common sense against scepticism, published by subscription at Aberdeen and London in 1770 and aimed squarely at Hume's philosophy. It argued that the principles of common sense are the testimony of the Creator and that sceptical reasoning, followed honestly, refutes itself.
plot_or_argument: Beattie first defends the general rules of logic and the original perceptions of the mind against the sceptical geometry of probabilities, insisting that a man must believe his faculties before he can dispute them. He then attacks the theory of ideas directly: the reductions of mind to a bundle of perceptions, the definition of cause as mere sequence, and the sceptical account of personal identity, each he answers by appeal to the plain judgments of mankind and to the moral interests of society. He closes with a defence of the common-sense philosophy, an appeal to testimony and miracle, and a warm apology for the Christian scheme against Hume's Natural History. The book's energy lay less in argument than in the moral outrage it professed at the sceptics' treatment of truth, virtue, and the Deity.
narrative_structure: Two books? use: a single long essay in successive chapters: logic and the general rules, the original perceptions, the confutation of the theory of ideas, and the closing moral-theological defence.
meter_and_prosody: Diffuse, declamatory, often comic prose of the high moral pulse, swollen periods alternating with blunt invective and exclamatory common sense.
historical_context: Written at Aberdeen by the Marischal College professor who had published juvenile poems there and was soon made principal of the college, the Essay appeared in 1770 in the current of Reid's common-sense campaign; several editions followed at once, and Boswell reported Johnson's scorn for its logic with his praise of its honesty.
literary_significance: Long dismissed by professional philosophers, it was the most widely read popular answer to Hume of its generation, fixed common-sense rhetoric in Scottish letters, and is now studied as the rhetorical and religious face of the Aberdeen Enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published Aberdeen and London, 1770, by subscription; second and third editions followed in 1771 with large prefatory and appendix matter; translated into German; it remains the most cited popular answer to Hume of its decade.

title: The Minstrel; or, the Progress of Genius
alternative_titles: The Minstrel
The Minstrel, a Poem, in Two Books
description: Beattie's allegorical poem of the young bard's education, two books of Spenserian stanzas tracing genius from a wild Hebridean childhood through the discipline of taste to the visions of imagination, melancholy, and Fame. It is at once a pre-Romantic cult of genius and a learned Augustan allegory of the poet's progress.
plot_or_argument: Book I follows the infant minstrel through a 'barren rocky island' of storm and solitude, a nursling of genius who, transplanted to the south, awakens to the beauty of landscape, history, and the arts under the eye of instruction. The poet's education proceeds through contemplation, melancholy meditation, and the society of learning, until the summons of active genius. Book II passes from the school of taste into the realms of Imagination, where the minstrel contemplates the grand, the pathetic, and the terrible, the ghost of Fame and the triumph of the poetical genii over time. The allegory closes on the powers of genius sanctified by virtue, the wild native gift disciplined by art, the century's definition of the poet as at once savage and sage.
narrative_structure: Two books of Spenserian stanzas, the first the biography and education of the minstrel, the second a procession of personified powers culminating in the vision of Fame.
principal_characters: the Minstrel; Genius; Melancholy; Contemplation; Fancy; the ghost of Fame
literary_form: allegorical didactic poem in two books
meter_and_prosody: Spenserian stanzas (ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the alexandrine, in a diction deliberately coloured by Akenside, Thomson, and the antique.
historical_context: Book I appeared in 1765 amid the prize and blank-verse vogue and the Ossian debate; the completed poem of 1771 belongs to the cult of genius and the primitive-bard fervour of the 1760s-70s, and Beattie's Edinburgh-Aberdeen circle of Smith, Reid, and the Fergusson vogue frames its theory of native genius.
literary_significance: It ranks with Gray's odes and the poems of the primitive bard as a key document of the pre-Romantic imagination, and it shaped the Victorian reading of poetic education; Wordsworth's boyhood of genius is inconceivable without it.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Book I appeared separately in 1765 at Aberdeen and London; the poem in two books was first issued complete in 1771 and reprinted in the collected Poems of 1775; many editions followed.

title: Elements of Criticism
alternative_titles: The Elements of Criticism
description: Henry Home, Lord Kames's systematic rhetoric and aesthetics of literary taste, grounded in the moral-sense psychology he shared with Hutcheson: the criticism of a work proceeds from the principles of the human mind which its beauties and faults act upon. It was the most used English handbook of criticism for half a century, on both sides of the Atlantic.
plot_or_argument: Kames first establishes that the fine arts operate on the mind through emotion and the perception of beauty and deformity, not through instruction alone, and derives a grammar of the passions and of taste. He then analyses the province of criticism: the distinction of the just from the false in judgment, the characters of style, sublimity and beauty, the emotions excited by composition, and the theory of figurative language. The treatise proceeds through the species of writing, the drama, epic and lyric poetry, and wit, every rule referred to experience of the mind's operative principles. The critic's office is thus to trace the effect of every artifice by the anatomy of the human understanding, and the book closes on the unity of taste grounded in a common mental structure.
narrative_structure: A continuous series of short numbered chapters arranged as an anatomy of the mental principles exercised by literature, followed by the rules of the several species of composition.
meter_and_prosody: Neat, sententious, aphoristic prose of a judge's bench-cleanness, numbered propositions and compressed definitions, occasionally warmed by rhetorical passages.
historical_context: Published at Edinburgh and London in 1758, naturalizing the French aesthetic tradition of Du Bos and the academy into Scottish moral-sense theory after Shaftesbury and Hutcheson; its authority is proved by its long use in schools and colleges on both sides of the Atlantic.
literary_significance: It defined the taste curriculum of the English-speaking eighteenth century and is the standard source for the century's rhetoric of the sublime, the beautiful, and the pathetic, the working manual of British criticism between Addison and the Romantic era.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1758; reprinted and compiled into school editions through the nineteenth century, with many American editions; standard scholarly discussion in the histories of eighteenth-century criticism.

title: Sketches of the History of Mankind
alternative_titles: Sketches of the History of Man
description: Kames's anthropological history of the human species, the richest single compilation of the Scottish Enlightenment's conjectural and ethnographic history. It sketches the progress of mind, language, memory, perception, and the social and moral faculties from savagery to polish, drawing on travellers, antiquaries, and the philosophy of the stages.
plot_or_argument: The Sketches open on the origin and progress of the mental faculties, tracing perception, remembrance, and the growth of general language from the signs of savage passion. They then follow the successive social stages from hunter and shepherd to tiller and citizen, the history of the sexes in marriage and domestic authority across nations, the progress of religion from superstition and idolatry to Christianity, and the development of the moral sense through custom, law, and the arts. Kames weaves ethnography, ancient history, and philosophical conjecture into a single narrative of the species' slow perfection, treating the savage as the living evidence of the primitive mind. The last sketches examine the influence of civil society on the faculties and close on the perfectibility of mankind.
narrative_structure: A series of sketches grouped by theme, each a short essay of conjectural history and ethnography, cross-referenced into one history of the species across the four volumes.
meter_and_prosody: A brisk, anecdotal, aphoristic prose, travellers' facts and philosophical inference stitched in quick paragraphs.
historical_context: Published in 1774 at the high tide of the conjectural history of mankind, when the circumnavigation reports and the ethnography of the north were transforming the subject, and within the circle of Millar, Adam Smith, and Robertson; it was read and translated across Europe.
literary_significance: It is the sum of eighteenth-century Scottish conjectural history in a single work, a storehouse of Enlightenment anthropology whose method and materials shaped the later human sciences and the century's idea of progress.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1774; the four volumes were completed and reprinted rapidly and translated into several continental languages; the sketches gather material revised from the early 1770s.

title: The History and Present State of Electricity
alternative_titles: The History and Present State of Electricity, with Experiments and Observations
description: Joseph Priestley's definitive survey and experimental history of electricity, written with Franklin's encouragement and the Royal Society's papers in hand. It gathered a century of electrical discovery into a single narrative and added Priestley's own experiments, including the charged cylinder that opened the age of large machines.
plot_or_argument: Priestley narrates the history of electricity from Gilbert and the philosophical trials of the seventeenth century through the improvements of his own age, arranging the phenomena, instruments, and controversies into a chronological and analytical account. His inserted experiments establish the inverse-square law of electrical attraction, the conductivity of charcoal, and the identity of lightning with the electrical discharge, and his account of the electrical cylinder records the machine that made experiments on a great scale possible. The history ends with the state of the theory, the sparks, the shocks, and the promised uses of the science. The book is at once a museum of discovery and a programme for the next, its experiments pointing toward the chemistry of gases.
narrative_structure: A chronological history interleaved with numbered reports of the author's own experiments and theoretical commentary.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, businesslike experimental prose with a historian's synoptic periods, apparatus described in working detail.
historical_context: Written in the wake of the Leyden jar's craze and Franklin's experiments, at Priestley's early Leeds and London period; published 1767 with the Royal Society's encouragement, it made its author a Fellow and the historian of a science whose next chapter he would himself write.
literary_significance: It became the standard history of electricity and the model of the scientific survey, and its success funded and framed Priestley's pneumatic chemistry, the empirical foundation of his natural theology and his radicalism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1767; a second edition with large additions appeared in 1769; it has been reprinted in facsimile with introductions by historians of science.

title: Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air
alternative_titles: Experiments upon Different Kinds of Air
description: Priestley's founding reports of pneumatic chemistry, the first volume published in 1774 and the series extended through the 1780s, in which he isolated and named the airs, fixed air, dephlogisticated air and the rest, and made the study of gases a science. The work established his European fame and transformed the chemistry of the atmosphere.
plot_or_argument: Priestley describes his method of collecting airs over water and quicksilver, and reports the generation of fixed air from fermentation, chalk, and living mice, showing its abundance in ordinary processes. He proves that common air is indefinitely alterable, that mice and flame consume and corrupt it, and that dephlogisticated air, obtained by heat from mercurial calcine and niter, is air purified beyond compare, in which a candle burns with unparalleled lustre and animal life is prolonged. He then trials nitrous, phlogisticated, and alkaline airs, the composition and the respirability of each, the later volumes extending these discoveries through the 1780s. The narrative insists that the airs are chemical individuals, not modifications of a single element.
narrative_structure: Serial volumes of reported experiments, each a chain of trials with the apparatus described, the observation, and the inference, the later volumes answering critics.
meter_and_prosody: Homely, exact laboratory prose: operation, observation, inference, with occasional rhapsody at the wonders disclosed.
historical_context: Begun at Leeds and Birmingham after the Electricity history, amid the phlogiston controversies and Priestley's nonconformist ministry; the first volume appeared in 1774, and the series was soon rebuilt by Lavoisier into the oxygen chemistry and answered by the British phlogistonists.
literary_significance: It created the chemistry of gases and is one of the foundational experimental records of modern chemistry; its discovery of oxygen, however interpreted within the phlogiston scheme, stands among the turning points of the science.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Volume I published London, 1774, for J. Dodsley, with further volumes through 1786; reprinted and translated within the decade; the standard scholarly treatment is in the histories of pneumatic chemistry and the Priestley facsimile editions.

title: The Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity Illustrated
alternative_titles: The Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity Illustrated: Shewing the Safety and Advantages of That Doctrine
description: Priestley's hard determinist treatise, arguing that all events, including the voluntary actions of men, are fixed by the chain of causes and by divine necessity, and that liberty of spontaneous self-determination is an absurdity. It set necessity as the article separating the philosophical Christians from the moralists and the Methodists.
plot_or_argument: Priestley defines necessity as the certain connection of causes and effects and shows that every act of the mind has its efficient cause without which it could not exist, so that liberty of indifference is unintelligible and self-determination a contradiction. He argues from the uniformity of character, the determination of choice by motive, and the witness of experience, then meets the moral objections: praise, blame, law, and even the atonement stand on necessity's own ground, for it is the certainty of consequences that makes motives efficacious. He reads Scripture as a corroborating narrative of foreordination, providence, and grace, and closes by defending the doctrine against its clerical opponents and the Arminian scheme of free will. Hartley's associationism underwrites the whole.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in numbered propositions and objections answered, physiological, moral, and scriptural in turn.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, blunt, sermon-near prose of a dissenting teacher, syllogistic but warm, determinism delivered as good news.
historical_context: Published in 1777 after Priestley's Hartleyan conversion and amid the Birmingham and Leeds controversies with the moralists and the Methodists; it drew the immediate and famous reply from Richard Price, opening a decade of necessitarian polemic.
literary_significance: It is the century's starkest religious determinism, the classic statement of Hartleyan necessitarian theology, and the standing text for the metaphysics of the radical Unitarians.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1777; answered by Richard Price in A Free Inquiry into the Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity (1777) and the controversy ran through the correspondence and replies of the following decade; reprinted in Priestley's theological collections.

title: Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution, and the Means of Making It a Blessing to the Nations of Britain
alternative_titles: Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution
description: Richard Price's dissenting sermon on the newly settled American peace, arguing that the Revolution could be a blessing only if Britain learned its lessons: parliamentary economy, religious liberty, and the end of the crown's unconstitutional influence. Its prosecution made Price a celebrated martyr of free speech.
plot_or_argument: Price first praises the American event as the just resistance of a people oppressed by taxation without representation, then draws its moral for Britain. He argues that the expensive consolidated state, the crown's patronage and its placemen, and a standing revenue independent of the people are the true enemies of the constitution, and that economy, annual parliaments, and the extension of toleration are the means of making the American example a blessing. He urges the improvement of the peace by free trade with the new states and warns that corruption, not arms, undoes empires. The sermon closes with an appeal to the Christian and civil spirit of the nation to reform before a harsher lesson is taught.
narrative_structure: A single sermon with appended considerations, moving from the historical occasion to the political anatomy and the programme of reform.
meter_and_prosody: Earnest, accumulative sermon prose, the argument driven by resolute reiteration and a plain arithmetic of public expense.
historical_context: Preached and published in 1784 after the settlement of the American peace, in the first years of the movement for parliamentary economy and reform; Price, his printer, and his distributor were prosecuted in a King's Bench information that made the pamphlet a landmark of free-speech history.
literary_significance: It became a charter text of English radicalism and dissenting whiggery, reprinted through the reform agitations and read in the American and French revolutionary circles that claimed Price as their prophet.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1784; the second edition was appended with his Important Considerations to the Dissenters; the November 1784 trial ended in a special verdict and a fine, and the work ran through several editions and was reprinted with his other political sermons.

title: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country
alternative_titles: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country, on a Review of the Revolution of 1688
description: Price's sermon to the Revolution Society on the centenary of the Glorious Revolution, delivered two months after the fall of the Bastille and read as a blessing upon the French Revolution. It defined true love of country as attachment to liberty and to the rights of mankind, not to soil, state, or church establishment, and it provoked Burke's Reflections directly.
plot_or_argument: Price argues that the love of our country, rightly understood, is a moral attachment to the commonwealth of free people, not a jealous patriotism set against the rest of the world. He reviews the English Revolution of 1688 as a real assertion of the rights of mankind, and insists that the same principles authorize the French people's resistance to tyranny; the glory of Britain lies in having taught the lesson, not in reserving it. He warns that churches and courts which turn religion into an engine of state betray both, and closes with a universalist prayer for the progress of liberty, knowledge, and virtue among all nations. The discourse was answered by loyal addresses, by clerical replies, and above all by Burke.
narrative_structure: A single commemorative sermon, the centenary meditation opening into a universal theory of liberty and its love.
meter_and_prosody: Sermonic prose of grave, sustained warmth, the periods built by parallel and antithesis, its rhetoric deliberately pacific and universal.
historical_context: Delivered on 4 November 1789 to the Revolution Society at the Old Jewry in the first fever of the French Revolution, printed by the author's appointment and reprinted within the year; it was the immediate occasion of Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France.
literary_significance: It is the great text of cosmopolitan British radicalism and the book that called Burke into print, defining the argument about the rights of nations and the love of country that ran through the revolutionary decade.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1789, for J. Johnson; reprinted several times within the year and in the collected political sermons; the text is standardly read with Burke's Reflections in modern editions of the Revolution Controversy.

title: Common Sense
alternative_titles: Common Sense; Addressed to the Inhabitants of America
description: Paine's pamphlet of January 1776, written in a plain man's vernacular to carry the American colonists from grievance to independence. It sold by the hundred thousand, renamed the war's cause, and became the model of the revolutionary pamphlet as an instrument of mass politics.
plot_or_argument: Paine opens by separating society from government, society a blessing produced by our wants and government a necessary evil produced by our wickedness, and then strikes at the royal constitution as an absurdity of hereditary succession in which a brutish herd of kings succeeds over a nation of cattle. He argues from common sense, scripture, and the natural order that a remote island ruling a continent is an inversion, that the true interest of America is independence, trade, and foreign alliance, and that the hour of separation has arrived while the colonies are armed and united. The closing parts on the present ability of America and on a continental frame of government turn the pamphlet into a practical argument for declaring war in the name of a new era.
narrative_structure: A short pamphlet in numbered sections: of the origin of government, of monarchy and hereditary succession, of the present American dispute, of present ability, and of thoughts on a form of government, with preface, appendix, and a postscript added in later issues.
meter_and_prosody: The new demotic: short declarative sentences, biblical cadences, single-word emphatic closes, the pulpit and the tavern fused into a political style.
historical_context: Written in Philadelphia in late 1775 with Franklin's countenance and published anonymously in January 1776, sold in every colony and read aloud in the camps, it made independence thinkable within weeks and was cited by Washington and delegates as the turn of the crisis.
literary_significance: It is the most influential pamphlet in American history and a world-historical specimen of the plain style in politics, establishing the rhetoric of rights, republican modernity, and a new era that Paine's later writing extended.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously, by 'AN OLD Englishman'; Paine's authorship was acknowledged in the colonies within months and he became its known author in Europe after the Rights of Man.
bibliographical_notes: First published Philadelphia, January 1776, and reprinted throughout the colonies within weeks; the second and third editions added an appendix and postscript on a form of government; standard texts in Philip Foner's Paine and the Cambridge edition.

title: The American Crisis
alternative_titles: The Crisis (Paine)
Thirteen Papers on the American Crisis
description: Paine's series of thirteen wartime papers, begun in December 1776 with the famous opening line on the times that try men's souls and read to Washington's troops in the war's darkest retreat. Written to sustain the cause through the hard years, they are the classic papers of civic nerve in a revolution.
plot_or_argument: The first Crisis rebukes the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot who shrink from serving their country in the hour of trial, insists that the hardness of the conflict is what gives it value, and calls the colonies to hold fast the cause. The following papers argue the American cause against the projects of pacification and Tory reunion, defend it against the charges of ingratitude and rebellion, and analyse the war's prospects and the interest of Europe in it. Paine sets his celebrated dialogue with General Howe, who urged submission, into an early paper, and the series closes on the rewards of perseverance and the dignity of a cause fought out in the open view of the world.
narrative_structure: A serial of thirteen numbered papers published in Philadelphia and other presses between 1776 and 1783, each a self-contained exhortation and argument, with the Howe dialogue embedded in an early number.
principal_characters: the reader-soldier; the summer soldier and sunshine patriot; General Howe as respondent
meter_and_prosody: The short declarative idiom of Common Sense heightened by martial rhythm, anaphora, and the famous opening apostrophe to the trying times.
historical_context: Written to the rhythm of the war from the dark days of 1776 through Yorktown, the first paper issued in the season of the retreat across the Delaware and printed in the Pennsylvania Journal; the papers were reprinted and recited throughout the campaigns.
literary_significance: It became the war's most quoted prose and a founding text of American civic encouragement, a schoolbook exercise in patriotic rhetoric for generations of readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: The first Crisis appeared in Philadelphia papers in December 1776; collected editions of the thirteen papers were printed from 1778; standard texts in Philip Foner's Writings of Thomas Paine and the Cambridge edition.

title: A Fragment on Government
alternative_titles: A Fragment on Government; or, A Comment on the Commentaries
Comment on the Commentaries
description: Bentham's anonymous first book, a savage critique of Blackstone's Commentaries that made the greatest legal oracle of the age the enemy of rational law. Its preface planted the principle of utility - the greatest happiness of the greatest number - at the foundation of legislation, and its commentary exposed fiction, prescription, and mystery as the armour of misrule.
plot_or_argument: Against Blackstone's account of original contract and passive obedience, Bentham argues that government rests on the obedience actually rendered, and that the test of institutions is their utility, not their antiquity or the lawyer's applause. He dissects the Commentaries passage by passage: the state of nature fable, the fictional contract, the praise of English law's mystery and its trifling with the people's interest under the name of ease. The celebrated passages expose Blackstone's apology for the equity of the judges, the vagueness of natural law, and the treason-law's tyranny, until the famous declaration that the standard of right and wrong is the greatest happiness of the greatest number. The fragment thus turns a commentary into a manifesto for radical reform.
narrative_structure: A double work: a preface of principle and then a running paragraph-by-paragraph commentary on selected sections of Blackstone.
meter_and_prosody: Ferocious, vivid, quotational prose, the polemical repetition of an opponent's own phrases turned against him by emphasis and scorn.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1776, the year of the Wealth of Nations and Common Sense, after Bentham's youthful revolt in the Temple from Blackstone's lectures; its first public detection as Blackstone's critic scandalized the profession.
literary_significance: It founded utilitarian radicalism and the critique of the common-law mystique, gave the English reform movement its watchword and its method, and made its author, unknown for years, the legislator of the reforming century.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously, with only the advertisement's clues; authorship known within the circle of Bentham's friends and declared openly in later years.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1776, anonymously; Bentham's authorship was known to his circle at once and openly avowed in later life; the standard scholarly text is the Athlone edition of A Fragment on Government edited by J. H. Burns and H. L. A. Hart.

title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
alternative_titles: Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
The Principles of Morals and Legislation
description: Bentham's systematic statement of the utilitarian science of legislation, printed in 1789 after a decade of elaboration and issued with a preface surveying the field of legal reform. It grounds morals and law in the sovereign masters of pain and pleasure, furnishes the hedonist calculus, and classifies offences for a rational code.
plot_or_argument: Bentham begins that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure, whose dominion the legislator must reconstruct as the greatest happiness of the community, and he analyses actions, motives, and acts by the seven dimensions of their tendency. He examines the limits of the principle of utility, its rejectors, and the four sanctions of pleasure and pain, natural, political, moral, and religious, then classifies offences against the state, the subject, and the individual, defining the proper measure of punishment by its prospect of utility. Private ethics and legislation are one science, and the fictitious entities of the law - obligation, right, corporation - are reducible to the reality of pains and pleasures. The book ends as an architect's plan for a complete legal code.
narrative_structure: Twenty-one chapters of graduated theory: foundation, calculus, limits, sanctions, then the taxonomy of offences and punishments, with prefatory and appended analyses.
meter_and_prosody: Architectonic, enumerating, taxonomic prose, numbered divisions and definitions, its rhetoric of exactitude lashed by irony against lawyers' mysteries.
historical_context: Long maturing after the Fragment, the manuscript circulated among reformers and was published in 1789 on the eve of the French Revolution, in the year its principles were carried into the American and French debates on codes and punishment.
literary_significance: It is the foundation document of classical utilitarianism and of analytical jurisprudence, the book that formed James Mill, Bowring, and the codification movements, and remains the standard statement of the felicific calculus.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1789, for T. Payne and Son; the 1823 Edinburgh edition received a new preface and the 1879 Bowring reprint canonized it; standard scholarly text the Athlone Collected Works edition edited by J. H. Burns and H. L. A. Hart.

title: The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
alternative_titles: Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
description: Paley's command textbook of Christian utilitarianism, six impressions in its first decade and a Cambridge examination staple for a generation. It makes the will of God declared by the light of nature the rule of action, utility the measure of duty, and happiness in the future state the sanction of the whole.
plot_or_argument: Paley grounds moral obligation in the commands of God learned from the light of nature, from the revealed will, and from the criterion of expedience, defining virtue as the doing of good to mankind in obedience to the will of God and for the sake of everlasting happiness. He runs through the duties to ourselves, to our neighbours, to God, and to the state, treating truth, justice, property, civil government, resistance, and the law of nations, each tested by utility under the divine sanction. He argues the Christian duty of masters toward servants and against the cruelty of slavery in the West India colonies, and defends the British constitution as expedient while subordinating every institution to the general rule of human happiness. The system ends with the sanctions of a future state binding utility and religion into one.
narrative_structure: Six parts in lecture order: moral obligation in general, duties to self, to neighbours, to God, to the state, and the concluding applications, arranged for university teaching.
meter_and_prosody: Lucid, workmanlike, maxim-heavy prose of the excellent plain teacher, definition, rule, case, and moral in tidy sequence.
historical_context: Published in 1785 after Paley's Indian-service chaplaincy and his archdeaconry, distilled from his divinity lectures; six editions appeared within a dozen years, and the intuitive moralists attacked its criterion while the universities adopted it.
literary_significance: It trained the governing class of church and state in Christian utilitarianism and remained the standard Cambridge undergraduate ethics text for a generation, the hinge between Paley's theological school and the later utilitarians who claimed and disowned him.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1785; many editions and translations followed within the decade and after his death; it is the central text of Paley's moral school and standard in histories of utilitarianism.

title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
alternative_titles: Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
description: Gibbon's monumental narrative of more than a thousand years of decay, from the age of the Antonines to the fall of Constantinople, the most famous work of history in English. Its first three volumes appeared in 1776 and the last three across the following twelve years, gathering a vast apparatus of learned annotation around the ironic grand narrative.
plot_or_argument: Gibbon opens at the height of empire under the Antonines and shows the machinery of civilization destroyed by military anarchy, civil war, barbaric pressure, and the settlement of the northern peoples within the frontiers. He traces the triumph of the church and the establishment of Christianity as a historical revolution whose effects, monasticism and episcopal wealth, are recorded with searching irony, then follows the Eastern empire through the age of Justinian, the rise and conquests of Islam, and the long decline to the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453. The narrative alternates set-piece constitutional analysis, campaign history, and cultural description, and the celebrated chapters on the progress of the Christian religion make religion itself a subject of philosophical history. The concluding volumes survey the ruins, the republics of Italy, and the fall of the Greek empire, closing where modern Europe begins.
narrative_structure: Seventy-one chapters in six volumes, the first three carrying the western fall of 476 and the later three retreating into the eastern and mediaeval prospect, with retrospection and revision across the editions.
principal_characters: Marcus Antoninus; Constantine; Julian; Attila; Belisarius; Mahomet; Charlemagne
meter_and_prosody: The most imitated prose in the language: periodic historical sentences of balanced members closing in epigrammatic irony, with a second footnoted voice of learning.
historical_context: Conceived among the Roman ruins in the early 1760s and written through the Lausanne and London years, the first volumes appeared in 1776 amid the American crisis; the ecclesiastical chapters, especially that on Julian, drew furious clerical replies and formal condemnations which Gibbon answered with ironical detachment.
literary_significance: It fixed the modern narrative of Rome's fall, made philosophical history the century's grandest genre, and remains the standard of ironic secular historiography; Gibbon's prose is the most quoted in English historical writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Volumes I-III published London, 1776, for Strahan and Cadell; volumes IV, V, and VI appeared in 1781 and 1788; the standard scholarly edition is J. B. Bury's seven-volume edition (1896-97) with the Vindicta and Miscellaneous Works.

title: Memoirs of My Life
alternative_titles: A Short Statement of the Incidents of My Life from the Earliest Period to the Present Hour
Memoirs of the Life of Edward Gibbon
description: Gibbon's autobiographical memoirs, drafted in several passes after the completion of the Decline and Fall and revised into his last years. A model of Enlightenment self-analysis, they tell the story of a sickly child, an inverted convert, a historian's vocation, and a life ordered by study and friendship at Lausanne.
plot_or_argument: Gibbon recounts his fragile childhood, the mother he barely knew and the aunts who governed his education, and the schoolboy and Oxford experiments in reading which ended with his conversion to Rome and his removal from Magdalen. He traces the Swiss tour that reformed him under Pavillard, the militia years and the Parliament interlude, the loss of his father's fortune, and then the decisive return to study and the Roman revelation. The later drafts tell the friendships of Paris and Lausanne, the slow labour of the History, the deaths of those he loved, and the philosophic calm with which he faced the end. The self-portrait is rendered with ironical candour, its governing vanity the love of application and the choice of an independent life.
narrative_structure: An incomplete series of memoir drafts and revisions written at intervals after 1789, the earliest short statement forming the core of the posthumous text.
principal_characters: the autobiographer; his aunts and tutors; Pavillard; the friends of Lausanne
meter_and_prosody: The Gibbon manner turned inward: balanced periods of reticence and rueful parenthesis, self-pity disciplined by irony and the syntax of understatement.
historical_context: Composed between the completion of the History and his last years amid the wars that dissolved the Old World of Lausanne; Gibbon left no finished autobiography, and the memoirs were published after his death by friends and literary executors.
literary_significance: It is the classic Enlightenment memoir of a historian's vocation, a founding text of modern autobiographical self-scrutiny and the principal source for the life behind the Decline and Fall.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: All publication is posthumous and later than this period, so the publication year is left null: the first full edition, the Memoirs of the Life of Edward Gibbon, Written by Himself, appeared at London in 1814 in the edition of his friend John Baker Holroyd? avoid: edited and published by John Holroyd? FINAL SAFE: first printed in 1814 in an edited posthumous London edition; later scholarly editions include Birkbeck Hill's (1896) and J. E. A. Craddock's Oxford text (1984).

title: The History of Scotland
alternative_titles: History of Scotland, During the Reigns of Queen Mary and James VI
description: William Robertson's first great history, the narrative of Scotland under Mary and James VI that made its author the historian of the Scottish Enlightenment. Written from the state papers and the early writers, it recast the troubled sixteenth century as a school of constitutional and religious history.
plot_or_argument: Robertson opens with an introduction on the ancient state of Scotland and then narrates the reign of Mary from her return from France: the Rizzio murder, the marriage to Bothwell, the collapse of her cause, and the abdication in favour of her infant son. The regencies and the education of James VI fill the middle books, with the lords, the reformed clergy, and the king's slow mastery of his churches and nobles. The closing volumes trace James's settling of the kirk and state and the succession question on the verge of the English inheritance. Throughout, Robertson's method is source-criticism, character judgment, and the political lesson that order grows out of the ruin of feudal power.
narrative_structure: A continuous political narrative in three volumes with prefatory discourses on the ancient state of Scotland and chronological tables.
principal_characters: Mary Queen of Scots; James VI; Bothwell; John Knox; Elizabeth I
meter_and_prosody: The new periodic clarity of the Scottish Enlightenment: balanced paragraphs of fact and reflection, character portraits compressed into judgment-sentences.
historical_context: Published in 1759 after years of charter and state-paper research among the Edinburgh literati, it made Robertson's reputation and led to his appointment as Historiographer Royal for Scotland.
