literary_significance: It created the scholarly narrative of Mary and the Scottish reformation on which all later debate has worked, and set the style of philosophical history in Britain.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1759, in three volumes; enlarged editions with corrections followed through the 1760s and 1770s; it remains the fountainhead of the Mary controversy in modern historiography.

title: The History of the Reign of the Emperor Charles V
alternative_titles: History of the Reign of Charles V
description: Robertson's imperial history of Charles V and the European states system, built on the Habsburg archival and printed materials he was among the first English historians to exploit. It made the age of the Reformation and the Habsburg-Valois wars intelligible as the birth of the modern balance of power, and became the most admired British history of the decade in several languages.
plot_or_argument: Robertson narrates the accession and inheritance of Charles, the rivalries with Francis I of France, the Turkish pressure on the empire, and the German religious division from Luther to the Peace of Augsburg, showing how the dream of universal monarchy collapsed against the particular liberties of princes and nations. He treats the Reformation as high politics: the leagues, the diets, the councils, the Schmalkaldic War, and the emperor's eventual weariness and abdication. The narrative constantly weighs the springs of state, the expedients of finance, and the maxims of a balancing Europe, in set-pieces on the constitutions of the continent. The history ends on the divided inheritance and the modern states system it left behind.
narrative_structure: A continuous political and military narrative in several volumes, with separate disquisitions on the state of Europe appended in the later editions.
principal_characters: Charles V; Francis I; Henry VIII; Luther; the princes of the Schmalkaldic League; Suleiman the Magnificent
meter_and_prosody: The mature philosophical style: capacious periods, weighty antithesis, and the judgment of cabinets, a prose of authority with a moralist's poise.
historical_context: Published in 1769 after Robertson's appointment as Historiographer Royal and years of archival research; it was translated into French, Italian, and German and read as a textbook of statecraft in the Atlantic world.
literary_significance: It defined the age of Charles V for generations of English readers, established the balance-of-power narrative of modern European history, and stood among the most admired works of the Scottish Enlightenment.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1769; the later volumes and editions carried the appended disquisitions; editions multiplied through the century, and it remained the standard English narrative of Charles V's reign.

title: The History of America
alternative_titles: History of America
description: Robertson's history of the Spanish discovery and settlement of America, the standard English account for a century, the first volumes appearing in 1777 and the later books on the other European colonies completed after his death. It turned the conquests and colonial histories into a philosophical narrative of the extension of Europe.
plot_or_argument: The narrative opens with the state of the American nations before 1492, their arts, governments, and religions treated with Robertson's blend of wonder and condescension, then follows Columbus from the enterprise to the governorship, the voyages, and the discovery of the mainland. It chronicles the conquest of Mexico and Peru with Cortes and Pizarro, the establishment of the Spanish colonial system, the treatment of the natives, and the rise of the other European colonies in North America and the West Indies. The closing volumes, completed after his death, carry the history of the British plantations, their constitutions, and the temper of the new societies. The whole reads as a science of colonies: climate, soil, constitution, and commerce explaining the destinies of the European America.
narrative_structure: Volumes published from 1777 with the later books completed after the author's death: the discovery, the Spanish conquests, and the northern colonies forming one history of America under Europe.
principal_characters: Columbus; Cortes; Pizarro; the American nations; the colonial projectors
meter_and_prosody: The capacious balanced periods of late philosophical history, campaign and constitution set in stately alternation with the moralist's clauses of judgment.
historical_context: Published from 1777 as the American revolution broke out, drawing on the historians of the Indies and the accumulated voyage literature; it stood at the centre of Robertson's late work as the great historical geographer of the Atlantic.
literary_significance: It was the received history of America in English well into the nineteenth century, the book through which generations read Columbus and the conquests, and a foundation of the historical geography of the Atlantic world.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Volumes on the Spanish discovery and conquests published London, 1777, for W. Strahan and T. Cadell; the history of the northern colonies was completed in the editions of the 1790s after Robertson's death; long standard and widely translated.

title: Hymns and Sacred Poems
alternative_titles: A Collection of Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739)
description: The first hymn book of the Wesleyan revival, published at Bristol in 1739 by the two brothers and containing Charles Wesley's earliest great hymns. Its preface marked the break with the Church of England and gave Methodism its programme of 'Scripture, Reason, and Experience' in worship.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers hymns for the seasons, sacraments, and occasions of Christian experience: the nativity and passion, the resurrection and ascension, justification, assurance, prayer, and the close of the year. Its poems move from the 'little flock' of the societies through calls to repentance to the triumphant hark of the wedding hymn and the self-dedicating 'Leave all thy self behind'. The preface defends extempore singing in the field assemblies, answers the charges of enthusiasm, and sets out the Wesleyan reading of salvation by faith. The collection establishes the pattern of the Methodist hymn book: experience sung in the first person plural.
narrative_structure: An ordered hymn collection with prefatory defence, the hymns arranged by Christian seasons and doctrinal heads rather than narrative.
principal_characters: the singing society; the Wesley family
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly common and long metre hymn stanzas of four and six lines in iambic measures, with the brothers' varied tunes indicated; the diction is deliberately plain and homiletic.
historical_context: Published at Bristol in 1739 in the first open-air season of the revival, after the Aldersgate year and the brothers' American voyage, as the field preaching needed its own songbook against the established psalmody.
literary_significance: It founded Methodist hymnody and introduced Charles Wesley's lyric voice, the most prolific and enduring hymn writer in English, into worship that spread through the Atlantic world.
attribution_notes: Joint collection of John and Charles Wesley; individual hymns are generally assignable, with Charles as author of the great majority.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Bristol in 1739; reissued and enlarged in the collections of the following decade; the standard account is in the histories of Methodist hymnody and in the variant-reading editions of Charles Wesley's hymns.

title: A Collection of Psalms and Hymns
alternative_titles: Psalms and Hymns (Wesley, 1738)
description: The Wesleys' first London hymn collection, issued in 1738 for the society they met with and drawing on the psalter versions and hymns then in use among the Oxford and London methodists. It carries the earliest printed fruits of Charles Wesley's hymnwriting alongside metrical psalms and the brothers' translations.
plot_or_argument: The collection sets David's psalms in metrical version beside hymns for the chief seasons and doctrines: Advent, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, repentance, faith, and the last things. Its prefatory address pleads the conscience of the writers in choosing and mending the old versions, and its hymns already display Charles's gift for first-person assurance and tender doctrine. The volume thus forms a bridge from the Psalm-singing of the Church of England to the full Methodist hymnody of the Bristol collections.
narrative_structure: A dual collection, psalms in metre followed by hymns arranged by seasons and subjects, with preface and occasional doxologies.
principal_characters: the London society
meter_and_prosody: Common, long, and short metre psalm stanzas and hymn measures of iambic lines; the language plain and singable, after the style of the earlier methodist psalmody.
historical_context: Published in London in 1738 in the months of Aldersgate and the societies' forming, after the Oxford Psalm and Hymn pocket book of 1733 and before the Bristol Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739.
literary_significance: It marks the moment the Wesleyan movement began to sing in print, the first public shape of the revival's lyric theology and the ancestor of the great Methodist collections.
attribution_notes: Prepared by John and Charles Wesley; Charles is the author of the new hymns, the psalter versions being collaborative and largely rehandled from earlier hands.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1738; a second edition followed within the year; discussed in every history of Methodist hymnody as the opening collection of the Wesleys' career as editors.

title: Hymns for the Nativity
alternative_titles: Hymns on the Nativity
description: Charles Wesley's season collection for Advent and Christmas, published at Bristol in 1745 and the turning-point in which his nativity hymns took their permanent forms, including the text of Hark! the Herald Angels Sing after the 1739 Harks! how the joyful voices sound. It is the most nearly complete single-occasion volume of eighteenth-century English hymnody.
plot_or_argument: The hymns run the Christian year's opening: the anticipation of the messiah, the forerunner, the annunciation, the birth in David's town, the shepherds, the wise men, the circumcision, and the presentation, closing with the childhood at Nazareth. Charles turns each scene into doctrine sung as experience, the little child and the mighty God joined in paradoxes of incarnation, and the season's joy poured out in invitation and praise. The volume's revision of the earlier wedding-hymn text set the pattern of Charles's practice of rewriting his own hymns toward their best forms. Its short songs for families and social worship make the Christmas narrative a domestic liturgy.
narrative_structure: A cycle of hymns following the gospel events of the nativity in seasonal order, with invitation, praise, and close-of-season pieces attached.
meter_and_prosody: Varied hymn measures, chiefly common metre and the eight-line 8s with refrain patterns, in tight iambic lines with Charles's characteristic internal rhyme and exclamatory openings.
historical_context: Published at Bristol in 1745, in the season of Charles Wesley's marriage and mature Bristol hymnwriting and the brothers' separate but parallel collections, when the revival's songbook was becoming a literature.
literary_significance: It gave the English-speaking churches their Christmas hymnody, the source of the most sung nativity text in the language, and remains the central exhibit of Charles Wesley's lyrical theology.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published Bristol, 1745; many hymns reissued in the later collections and in A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People called Methodists (1780); critical texts in the variant editions of Charles Wesley's hymns.

title: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling
alternative_titles: A Hymn for the Inner Room
description: Charles Wesley's great hymn of sanctifying love, a short lyric in which the soul prays to be bound to its Lord and made all the love it beholds. It stands among the most admired hymns in English and among the highest achievements of Charles Wesley's later Bristol period.
plot_or_argument: The hymn opens on the captive soul's address to divine love, fixed and bound by the bands of its own choosing, and moves through petition for the lamp of pure flame and anticipation of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Its central desire is entire consecration, that the heart be fixed, abiding, and cleaving to its God, and the closing stanzas ask the loss of self in God, the soul dyed with the love of Christ, and a close in praise. The argument is Methodist perfectionism turned into lyric yearning, doctrine as amorous address. Each stanza advances the surrender one degree farther toward the wish to be all love.
narrative_structure: A single continuous lyric in six stanzas, from captivity and petition to union and doxology.
meter_and_prosody: Stanzas of the eight-syllable trochaic seven-line measure known in hymnals as 7.7.7.7.7.7.7, with paired internal rhymes that give the verse its urgency; the received text runs to six stanzas and is now sung to tunes such as HYFRYDOL and NICAEA.
historical_context: Composed at Bristol in 1762, in Charles Wesley's mature season of hymns for the societies' social worship and the inner room, the year of his wife's death and of some of his deepest lyrics, though the hymn's own first appearance is disputed among the small collections of these years.
literary_significance: A summit of English hymnody and of the lyric of religious desire, anthologized universally and the model of the Methodist sanctification hymn; its imagery shaped later devotional verse and hymn-tune pairing.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: Composition is securely dated to 1762 by Charles Wesley's own practice and the society's usage; its first printing is complicated by the reissues and re-numberings of the small Bristol collections of 1762-63, so the publication year is left null here; the canonical text is that of the collected Poems on Several Occasions and of A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People called Methodists, 1780.

title: Explanatory Notes Upon the New Testament
alternative_titles: Wesley's Explanatory Notes on the New Testament
description: John Wesley's one-volume commentary on the New Testament, verse by verse, the most widely circulating English exegesis of Methodism and a deliberate distillation of Bengelius, Grotius, Lightfoot, and the practical writers. It gave the preachers and a lay readership a complete working interpretation of the text in English.
plot_or_argument: Wesley prints the received English text in sense paragraphs and follows each verse with notes that paraphrase, clear the idiom, weigh the sense against other translators, and press the practical and experimental meaning. The notes are strongest on justification by faith, assurance, inward sanctification, and Christian perfection, doctrines he reads through the whole of the epistles and Gospels; he handles prophecy, the church, and the sacraments with a return to primitive antiquity. Difficulties of gospel chronology and the Pauline argument receive plain, workmanlike solutions. The whole is a manual of the New Testament made for preachers on horseback and pious families.
narrative_structure: A continuous verse commentary on the books of the New Testament in canonical order, paragraph by paragraph.
meter_and_prosody: Condensed, abbreviated note prose of marginal shorthand made discursive, its sentences pared to the practical point.
historical_context: Produced in the thick of Wesley's preaching ministry and the society's growth, published in 1754 for the use of the Methodists, it gathered earlier continental and English annotation into a standard of Methodist scriptural reason joined to heart-religion.
literary_significance: It became the working New Testament of early Methodism on both sides of the Atlantic and remains the fullest witness to Wesley's exegetical mind and his doctrine of experimental religion.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1754; reissued repeatedly into the nineteenth century alongside the hymns and the journal; modern reprints serve Methodist study and the history of exegesis.

title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
alternative_titles: The Methodist Hymn Book of 1780
description: John Wesley's canonical hymnal, gathered from the brothers' earlier collections into some five hundred and twenty-five hymns, his last great editorial act and the book Methodism long sang from. He meant it as a compact scripture of heart and doctrine, its order teaching the whole Methodist way of salvation in verse.
plot_or_argument: The collection orders the Christian and Methodist life from general hymns of praise through the acts and sufferings of Christ, the operations of the Spirit, the states of the believer, the means of grace, the sacraments, and the seasons of the year, a walk through divinity in song. Its nucleus is Charles Wesley's lyric theology, with the best of Watts, Doddridge, and the older hymnists admitted beside John's own translations and paraphrases. The editor pruned, altered, and regularized the texts of forty revival years into a single honest compass of experimental religion. Its preface states the design plainly: that the people called Methodists should own the whole of their religion and hope in one small book they could sing.
narrative_structure: An ordered hymnal in heads following the course of divinity and the church year, with preface and indices by subject and first line.
meter_and_prosody: The common, long, short, and varied eight-line hymn metres of Augustan psalmody, the texts regularized in diction and measure by the editor.
historical_context: Published in 1780 as the societies entered the last decade under John Wesley's sole governance, it deliberately canonized the revival's song against the multiplicity of earlier collections and became the standard of Methodist worship.
literary_significance: It is the parent of almost all later Methodist hymnals and one of the most influential hymn books in the language, fixing the canon of Charles Wesley's lyrics in the worship of the whole communion.
attribution_notes: Edited throughout by John Wesley; the majority of hymns are Charles Wesley's, with others by Watts, Doddridge, and earlier hands.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1780; its texts and variants are studied in the histories of Methodist hymnody and in the edition of Charles Wesley's hymns with variant readings; it passed into the later Methodist denominations' hymnals.

title: A Short Account of God's Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield
alternative_titles: God's Dealings with George Whitefield
An Account of the Life of the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield (1739 edition)
description: Whitefield's spiritual autobiography, first printed in Philadelphia and enlarged in a Dublin edition of 1740 with a preface by John Wesley. It told the story of the conversion of an orphaned tallow-chandler's apprentice into the field preacher of three continents, the most read conversion narrative of the evangelical revival.
plot_or_argument: Whitefield recounts his boyhood at the Bell Inn in Gloucester, the Oxford years with the Wesleys and the Holy Club, and the methodist disciplines of fasting, communion, and service in the prisons. He tells of his conversion through a book on the meritorious blood and righteousness of Christ, the moment he knew himself a child of God, and the fervour that followed into ordination and the sermon at Cincinnati? no: into his first American journey and the open-air field. The narrative weighs each experience against scripture, giving the Word as the evidence of every inward turn, and closes on the providence that carried the preacher from closed pulpits to the multitudes of the fields.
narrative_structure: A continuous conversion narrative from childhood through conversion to apostolic call, framed by Wesley's prefatory endorsement in the Dublin issue.
principal_characters: George Whitefield as narrator; John and Charles Wesley; the Oxford club
meter_and_prosody: Earnest, plain, exclamatory autobiographical prose, biblical quotation as the measure and sanction of every stated feeling.
historical_context: Published in the first Atlantic season of the revival, 1739-40, as Whitefield's field preaching and his American journey made him the transatlantic evangelist; its printing by Franklin in Philadelphia? use: its American printing in 1739 and Wesley's Dublin preface in 1740 secured its wide circulation.
literary_significance: It gave the evangelical revival its canonical conversion plot and made the autobiography of grace a mass genre; it remains the primary source for the Holy Club and the origins of Methodism in open air.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Philadelphia in 1739; the enlarged Dublin edition of 1740 carried John Wesley's prefatory address; editions and translations followed in London and across the Atlantic world, and it is a standard source in histories of the evangelical revival.

title: The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul
alternative_titles: The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul, in Two Parts
description: Doddridge's classic account of experimental religion in the soul, a series of discourses with letters and meditations, published in 1745 and the most used Protestant guide to conversion, self-examination, and growth in grace between Bunyan and the Victorian evangelicals. Its careful cadence of assurance made it a standard of moderate dissenting piety.
plot_or_argument: The discourses trace the sinner's progress from awakening under the sense of divine justice, through conversion, justification, adoption, and sanctification, to the believer's combat with remaining corruption and the assurance of hope. Doddridge balances the enthusiast's heat and the formalist's cold, prescribing self-examination, the duties of the closet, and the improvement of reason joined to the affections. Interposed letters and meditations carry the same lesson into the hours of the day and the table of the Lord. The whole is a Protestant pilgrimage of the soul in sermon form, its aim, in his phrase, experimental and practical religion.
narrative_structure: A series of discourses on the stages of salvation in the soul, interspersed with letters, meditations, and prayers for daily use.
meter_and_prosody: The balanced, affectionate sermon-cadence of the high dissenting style, periodic sentences of tenderness with psalm quotation and doxology.
historical_context: Composed across the Northampton academy years, parts appearing from the later 1730s and the whole published at London in 1745, in the debate over enthusiasm and experimental religion opened by Whitefield and carried on by the moderates.
literary_significance: It trained generations of evangelicals, dissenters, and Methodists in the phenomenology of grace, ran through countless editions and translations, and shaped the devotional literature of the English-speaking Protestant world.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published in full at London, 1745, after parts had appeared in the earlier magazines; editions, American reprints, and translations multiplied through the following century.

title: The Family Expositor
alternative_titles: The Family Expositor: or, A Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament
description: Doddridge's great posthumous work, a paraphrase and commentary on the New Testament in weekly family portions, published from his manuscripts from 1756 into the 1760s. It was designed to make each section of scripture a complete act of family worship: text, sense, improvement, and devotion together.
plot_or_argument: Each week's portion gives the biblical text with a running paraphrase that supplies the idioms and links, a commentary of doctrine and criticism, and then the practical improvement for the heart and life. Doddridge draws on the best earlier annotators, joining scholarship of a learned temper to pulpit directness. The improvements turn each passage into meditation on providence, the Saviour's love, and the duties of the common hour. The work runs its course through the Gospels and Acts into the epistles, the later volumes completed from his papers by friends.
narrative_structure: A continuous paraphrase-commentary in weekly family lessons through the books of the New Testament, each lesson a unit of text, paraphrase, comment, and improvement.
meter_and_prosody: A smooth, meditative prose of paraphrase and application, the rhythms of prayer woven into exposition.
historical_context: Long prepared at Northampton for the academy and for the family devotions of his people, and published after his death from 1756, it became the most popular Protestant family New Testament of the later eighteenth century.
literary_significance: It set the model of the devotional commentary for family worship and, through its completion and constant reprinting into the nineteenth century, formed generations of Protestant reading of the New Testament.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1756 onward in six volumes, the later volumes prepared from Doddridge's manuscripts with the assistance of friends; editions with improvements ran well into the nineteenth century.

title: Hymns and Spiritual Songs
alternative_titles: Hymns and Spiritual Songs, in Three Books
description: Isaac Watts's first hymn collection, three books of Scriptural, moral, and devotional songs, the foundation of English hymnody as a literate genre. Its preface argued the duty and privilege of singing 'new songs under the gospel dispensation' and freed nonconformist worship from the exclusive metrical psalter.
plot_or_argument: Book I sings selected Scriptures into verse, psalm and canticle paraphrase with didactic edges; Book II offers moral and divine subjects, the temper of the soul, death, judgment, and grace; Book III gathers divine songs of a more spiritual and affectionate cast, the longest and most quoted. Watts moves the hymn from catechism to meditation, making the first person plural of the church the voice of the awakened individual. Its best texts, from the drowsy falling sleep of the slumbering Jesus to the cross, the throne, and the coming of the Lord, became staples of every later collection. The whole carries the Puritan sermon into tuneful, rationally ordered praise.
narrative_structure: Three books arranged by source and subject, the later books progressively more experimental, with preface defending gospel hymnody.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly common, short, and long metre iambic stanzas of Augustan psalmody, plain diction, strong syntax, and the memorable simple phrase.
historical_context: Published in London in 1707 with the author's early independent-ministry years at Bury and London behind it, in the reforming decade when dissent began to sing hymns of modern composition beside Sternhold and Hopkins.
literary_significance: Watts is 'the father of English hymnody' and this book the charter document, the collection from which the English-speaking churches have most drawn their songs of worship through three centuries.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1707; enlarged and reordered editions appeared under his eye, and the collected Poems, Religious and Moral, followed in 1724; its hymns passed into every subsequent English hymnal.

title: Divine and Moral Songs for the Use of Children
alternative_titles: Divine and Moral Songs for Children
description: Watts's hymnal for children, the first English collection written in and for the childhood of the Christian family, divided into divine songs for children of the first and second degree and moral songs on duties and gentlenesses of life. It made childhood a subject and an audience of evangelical literature.
plot_or_argument: The divine songs bring doctrine home to little capacities: God's glory seen in the world, the Saviour as friend of children, repentance, prayer before and after sleep, and the care of the season of youth. The moral songs teach temperance, cleanliness, truth, kindness to beasts and servants, the use of time, and the government of the tongue. Watts writes with the double voice of tenderness and fear, the child's own speech joined to a warn? use: joined to parental awe. The collection became the ordinary prayer-and-praise book of Victorian nurseries and the model of all child-evangelical verse.
narrative_structure: A graduated collection in two main classes, divine and moral songs, subdivided by the age of the child, each poem one lesson of heart or conduct.
meter_and_prosody: Short iambic common and short measures of nursery simplicity, direct address and little rhymes of the most lucid Augustan plain style.
historical_context: Published in London in 1715, the fruit of Watts's catechetical teaching in his congregations and of the new dissenting attention to children's education, a decade before the century's child-literature boom.
literary_significance: It founded the literature of childhood in English Nonconformity and gave the nursery its first canon of hymns; its influence runs through every later children's religious book to the Victorian period.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1715; reissued in innumerable editions, often abridged and recast; still read in the histories of children's literature as the opening text of the genre.

title: The Psalms of David Imitated in the Christian Stile
alternative_titles: The Psalms of David Imitated in the New Testament Stile
Watts's Psalms
description: Isaac Watts's Christianizing paraphrase of the whole psalter, published in 1719 after controversy in his own congregation, the book that gave English Nonconformity its psalmody and gave the churches Joy to the World, When All Thy-Gods? safer: Ps. xciii and the Messiah hymns. It is Augustan hymnwriting at its most ambitious.
plot_or_argument: Watts paraphrases each psalm into gospel idiom, letting David speak of Christ, the church, and the believer's experience rather than only of Israel and Judah. The Advent and Nativity songs, the triumphs of providence, and the penitential psalms are rewritten into hymns of praise and instruction for Christian assemblies. His version of the one hundred and Ninety-third? FINAL: his paraphrase of Psalm 98 gave the churches Joy to the World, and the Advent and Messianic versions supplied the most used hymns in the language. The preface answers the strict psalm-singers, pleading that the gospel is new matter for praise and that David's songs must be read with Christian eyes.
narrative_structure: A continuous Christianizing paraphrase of the psalter, the longer psalms divided into numbered versions with hymns interspersed on gospel occasions.
meter_and_prosody: Command of the psalm and hymn metres of the early eighteenth century, with the expanded six and eight-line stanzas of his happiest odes, the diction elevated, sensuous, and plain at once.
historical_context: Published in London in 1719 after long argument in his own congregation over hymn-singing and in the season of the psalms controversy that divided older and younger Nonconformity; a large subscription volume announced by its author in his earlier Hymns.
literary_significance: It dominated the psalmody of English Nonconformity for a century and supplied hymns still sung everywhere, and it fixed the method of gospel paraphrase that later psalters and hymnals inherited.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1719, a large folio subscription edition; second and later editions followed; selections from it entered nearly every nineteenth-century hymnal.

title: Meditations among the Tombs
alternative_titles: Meditations and Devotions (collection including the Tombs meditation)
description: James Hervey's graveyard meditation, first printed in a London newspaper in 1746 and among the earliest classics of the graveyard school in prose. It passes from the dead to the living, from bones and monuments to faith, hope, and the resurrection.
plot_or_argument: The meditant walks the churchyard at twilight, addressing the tombs, the ashes, and the names of the buried, and moralizing on the levelling vanity of rank and beauty. The scene turns from desolation to consolation: the believer reads the graves as pledges of the resurrection and the dust of the fathers as sleep, and the meditation rises through hope of immortality to a triumphant close on the day when death is swallowed up in victory. Hervey alternates the gloom of the night-piece with the rapture of gospel assurance, the fear and the feast of a funeral sermon turned into essay.
narrative_structure: A single continuous meditation moving from dusk to hope through the stations of the churchyard.
meter_and_prosody: Solemn, periodic, rhapsodic prose of the preromantic manner, long cadences of gloom broken by exclamatory uplift and hymn-like fragments.
historical_context: First printed in the General Evening Post in 1746 amid the vogue of the melancholy meditation and the grave-yard poetry of the decade, within the religious world the evangelical revival and the churchyard school shared.
literary_significance: It became the prose exemplar of the graveyard meditation, widely reprinted and praised by Johnson for its music, the bridge between the funeral sermon and preromantic grave-yard poetry.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1746 and collected in Hervey's Meditations and Devotions (1750); reprinted endlessly in the author's poetical and devotional collections and in anthologies.

title: Theron and Aspasio; or, A Scriptural and Critical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians
alternative_titles: Theron and Aspasio
description: James Hervey's devotional-argumentative masterpiece, issued in three volumes in 1755, casts the doctrines of grace and the righteousness of faith into a frame of letters, dialogues and a running commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Its ornate, balanced prose was admired across denominational lines even by readers who disliked its Calvinism. The work immediately became the occasion of John Wesley's furious reply, because Wesley read its teaching on justification as antinomian and disparaging of holiness of life.
plot_or_argument: The letters and dialogues between Aspasio, a Christian nobleman, and his friend Theron trace the grounds of natural religion, the corruption of human nature, and the necessity of an imputed righteousness. Hervey then appends a scriptural and critical commentary on Galatians, arguing that the epistle establishes justification by faith alone and excludes all human boasting. The intermediate dialogues dramatise the contrast between a moralist religion of self-effort and a gospel religion of reliance on Christ, and press home the practical duties of the regenerate life. The whole is designed to be at once devotional reading, doctrinal instruction, and exegetical argument, and to show that profound Calvinism can be spoken in the most polished and affecting English.
narrative_structure: Three volumes arranged as a sequence of letters and dialogues framing a verse-by-verse commentary on Galatians, so that meditation, conversation and exegesis alternate throughout.
principal_characters: Aspasio; Theron
literary_form: Prose devotional and doctrinal treatise in epistolary and dialogic form with embedded biblical commentary
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a highly wrought periodic style of balanced clauses and cadenced rhythm
historical_context: Published in the middle of the Calvinistic-Arminian revival controversies, the book belongs to the effusive piety associated with the Countess of Huntingdon's connection and to Hervey's own late meditations at Weston underoclic. It also belongs to the broader eighteenth-century fashion for ornamental religious prose and to the growing use of dialogue and epistle as vehicles for theological argument.
literary_significance: For a century Theron and Aspasio was quoted as a model of English religious prose, and Samuel Johnson and Robert Hall admired its eloquence. Its publication provoked one of the most energetic pamphlet exchanges of the century, Wesley's Defense of his own letter and the long controversy with the label "Calvinism" attached to it. The book remains the clearest instance of how evangelical doctrine could be accommodated to polite Augustan diction.
attribution_notes: Authorship by James Hervey is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published in three volumes, London, 1755, and frequently reprinted, often with the shorter title Theron and Aspasio; a revised edition appeared in 1768.

title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne, in the County of Hampshire
alternative_titles: The Natural History of Selborne
description: The published form of a long correspondence between the country naturalist Gilbert White and his friends Daines Barrington and Thomas Pennant, The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne records the seasons, weather, birds, mammals, insects and parish antiquities of one Hampshire village. Its method is patient first-hand observation entered in a memoranda book and then shaped into familiar letters. The result is the founding text of English phenomenological nature-writing and a classic of empirical natural history.
plot_or_argument: White surveys the natural history of Selborne parish under a sequence of heads: the zoology of its vertebrates and invertebrates, the periodical return of migrations, the phenomena of hibernation in bats, the structure of swallows' nests, and the monthly calendar of appearance. Interwoven are antiquarian notices of the parish and its manors, and the weather-journal whose measurements anchor the whole. From these particulars he draws general conclusions about instinct, the economy of nature, and the value of quantitative records kept over many years.
narrative_structure: Two parts in the form of letters to two correspondents, arranged topically rather than narratively, with the weather journal and observations woven as enumerated particulars.
principal_characters: Gilbert White; Daines Barrington; Thomas Pennant
literary_form: Epistolary natural history and antiquarian survey in familiar letters
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in an unadorned, precise, quietly humorous plain style
historical_context: The book belongs to the late-eighteenth-century vogue for parish-level natural history, for systematic weather observation, and for correspondence networks among gentleman-naturalists; it also reflects the Linnlean and Buffonian taxonomy then current and the antiquarian culture of the Society of Antiquaries.
literary_significance: It has never been out of print and is read both as a scientific classic, for its accurate records and its early treatment of hibernation and migration, and as a literary model of the observed particular. It set the manner of all later English nature-writing from Richard Jefferies to Laurie Lee, and it is a key document of the empirical, descriptive temper that eighteenth-century natural philosophy bequeathed to Romantic-era writing about the external world.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Gilbert White is established; the letters were edited for the press by his brother Revd Dr Thomas White, whose editorial hand is documented but does not displace Gilbert's authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1789, in octavo; a second edition appeared in 1790 and the standard modern edition is W. S. B. Lewis's (1993).

title: The Loves of the Plants
description: A didactic poem in four cantos which translates the Linnaean sexual system of botany into a pageant of personified flowers, each plant's reproductive organs rendered as the amours of a nymph and her swain. It first appeared in 1789 and was then issued as the second part of The Botanic Garden in 1791, and its brilliance, obscurity and frank eroticism made it at once a bestseller and a scandal. Erasmus Darwin supplies scientific matter in the accompanying notes, where he argues the vegetable kingdom's real structure.
plot_or_argument: The poem passes in sequence through the classes and orders of the Linnaean system, dramatising each as an allegorical courtship or marriage: the polyandrous female fern, the mutual fidelity of the flax, the violent loves of the poppy, the priestly solemnities of the mosses. Beneath the gallantry runs a serious argument about irritability, the contrivances of pollination, and the vegetable physiology revealed by microscopical enquiry. The closing canto turns from the floral court to the great powers of nature and to a deist hymn to universal benevolence, binding vegetable life into a general economy of heat, light and growth.
narrative_structure: Four cantos of linked ekphrastic episodes arranged by Linnaean class and order, with a scientific apparatus of prose notes appended to each.
principal_characters: Venus or the presiding goddess of the garden; personified plant-nymphs; sylphs and gnomes of the floral courts
literary_form: Didactic and descriptive verse in heroic couplets with prose scientific notes
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, variably decorated with lyric intercalations, imitation of air-sounds and insect-music
historical_context: Written in the Derby-Lichfield circle of erasmian natural philosophy and popular science, it transmits Linnaeus through translation and the sexual politics of the 1780s, amid the Botanical Society vogue, Erasmus Darwin's own zoonomic researches, and the radical Dissenting enthusiasm for progress and abolition.
literary_significance: The most influential English poem on botany, it shaped a generation's reading of Linnaeus and supplied the ornamental scientific vocabulary later parodied and admired. Coleridge and Southey acknowledged its example and Wordsworth's protest against personification is partly aimed at it; its mixture of erotic allegory and apparatus of notes is a distinctive late-Augustan solution to the problem of didactic form.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Erasmus Darwin is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1789, as the second part of The Botanic Garden; the joint first edition of both parts appeared in 1791, and the accompanying poem The Economy of Vegetation belongs to that later volume and to the nineteenth century.

title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by Himself
alternative_titles: The Interesting Narrative
The Life of Olaudah Equiano
description: The first great slave narrative in English, published in two volumes in 1789 and subscribed by hundreds of readers, including members of the royal family. Equiano tells of his childhood in Africa, his kidnapping and sale, the Middle Passage, twenty years of slavery and service in the Royal Navy and the merchant trade, his purchase of his own freedom, and his conversion and public anti-slavery activism. The narrative combines autobiography, travel writing, commercial detail and protest, and it became the most widely used text of the abolitionist campaign.
plot_or_argument: From an idealised account of Igbo society in what is now Nigeria the narrative moves to the horror of the middle passage, where the close-packing, mortality and torture of the ship are registered with precise numbers. Enslaved in the West Indies and then in England, Equiano serves the Royal Navy officer Michael Henry Pascal, is christened Gustavus Vassa by the Shipley family at Guernsey, works as a domestic servant and ship's crewman, and under the Philadelphia merchant Robert King learns bookkeeping and accumulates enough to buy his freedom in 1766. Later volumes recount his travels in the Arctic, Central America and Jamaica, his evangelical conversion and his circle of Methodist and Calvinistic friends, and a closing appeal to the imagination of British readers, in which the suffering of enslaved people is figured in the language of familial and Christian sympathy.
narrative_structure: Two-volume spiritual and commercial autobiography in chronological order, with a frame of providential design and a final section of documents, testimonials and abolitionist argument.
principal_characters: Michael Henry Pascal; Robert King; Granville Sharp; the Shipley family
literary_form: Autobiographical slave narrative with embedded travel journal and polemic
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, periodically structured narrative style with biblical and sentimental cadences
historical_context: Published in the year of the first abolitionist petition to Parliament and of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, it belongs to the evangelical and Quaker anti-slavery movement, to the boom in spiritual autobiography, and to the eighteenth-century literature of travel, commerce and natural history.
literary_significance: It established the conventions of the English-speaking slave narrative, the testimony of an authenticated self that refutes the theory of African incapacity. Its argument from felt sympathy, commercial evidence and Christian providence made it a decisive instrument of public persuasion and it is now a central text of eighteenth-century studies, of Atlantic history and of life-writing.
attribution_notes: Equiano's own authorship is accepted, though the degree of editorial help from abolitionist friends such as the bookseller and clergyman supporters is debated. Vincent Carretta has argued from contemporary records that Equiano may have been born in the British colonies rather than in Africa, which would make the opening African childhood a persuasive fiction; the narrative's factual status remains contested even where its authorship is not.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1789, two volumes, by the author and printed for the several booksellers named in the proposal; the standard modern editions are Vincent Carretta's (Penguin, 1995) and Robert J. Allison's (Bedford/St. Martin's, 1996). The date of composition is not established and is therefore left null.

title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Justice of Great Britain by the Africans
alternative_titles: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery
description: An abolitionist polemic by Ottobah Cugoano, a Fante man kidnapped and sold in 1769, who by the 1780s was a literate servant in the London household of the artist Richard Cosway. The book argues from natural law, scripture and British law that the slave trade and West Indian slavery are crimes against God and humanity, and it demands immediate remedy rather than gradual relief. A short abridgement for wider circulation followed in the same year, and a second edition with an appendix on the slave insurrection in Jamaica appeared in 1788.
plot_or_argument: Cugoano first states the natural right of every human being to liberty, so that enslavement is a violation of the law of God written on the conscience. He then examines the scriptural evidence and shows that neither Hebraic servitude nor the New Testament's household codes sanction the modern traffic, and he presses the legal argument that a Christian cannot lawfully hold a fellow Christian in perpetual slavery. Turning to practice, he denounces the planters' plea of necessity and property, refutes the political arithmetic that counts colonial wealth as national strength, and proposes remedies: the recall of British subjects from the colonies, the education of the enslaved, and the establishment of lawful commerce in Africa in place of the trade in persons. The conclusion warns that Britain's national guilt for the trade will draw national judgment.
narrative_structure: Continuous argumentative treatise in short numbered sections, moving from first principles to scriptural, legal and commercial refutation and then to proposals for remedy.
literary_form: Polemical essay in natural-law, scriptural and legal argument
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in an urgent, latinate, sermon-like style marked by biblical cadence
historical_context: Written between the Somersett decision of 1772 and the first parliamentary abolitionist campaign of 1788, it joins the printed output of the Committee for Abolishing the Slave Trade and the black London community of Equiano, Sharp and Ramsay, and reflects the evangelical moral-language of natural rights then current.
literary_significance: It is the first published abolitionist argument written by an African in England to confront the slave trade as a national crime and to claim the authority of reason and scripture against the planters' case. Its insistence that liberty is a divine and natural right, and its refusal of gradualist compromise, make it a foundational text of black Atlantic political writing and a necessary companion to Equiano's narrative.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Cugoano is accepted; the extent of assistance from friends and patrons in a household of artists and literati is discussed but does not displace his authorship, which the text signs as an African speaking for Africans.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1787, for S. and J. Leigh; an abridgement entitled Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery appeared the same year and a second edition with an appendix on the Jamaican insurrection in 1788. The standard edition is Patrick Fagan's (1999).

title: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery; or, of Admitting the Least Claim of Private Property in the Persons of Men, in England
alternative_titles: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery
description: The founding document of Granville Sharp's anti-slavery campaign, addressed to the merchants and planters of Great Britain and printed in London in 1769. Sharp, a clerk in the York Office and a self-taught Hebraist and grammarian, brings together biblical, legal and moral evidence that no master can hold a Christian as property, and warns that tolerating slavery corrupts English law and religion alike. Its learning, heat and long appendices of evidence made it the reference text of the British abolitionist case before Somersett's case of 1772.
plot_or_argument: Sharp argues first from scripture that the Old Testament's servitude laws are not the modern form of chattel slavery, and that the gospel, which forbids men to rule over conscience, condemns holding human beings as goods and chattels. He then reviews English law and the earlier decisions against villeinage and imported servitude, urging that no custom or statute within England can authorise property in the persons of men. He next examines the planters' pleas of commerce, necessity and colonial prescription, treating them as interests against justice; and closes with a plain remonstrance to slave-owners, inviting them to manumit voluntarily before the law or divine judgment compels them. The volume appends testimony about the treatment of slaves in the colonies and a grammatical and critical disquisition much of which concerns the Hebrew and Greek terms for servitude.
narrative_structure: Single sustained address in numbered argumentative divisions, followed by appended evidence, testimony and philological notes.
literary_form: Polemical and legal-religious treatise addressed as a public representation
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, lawyerly and scriptural register
historical_context: Written in the decade of the Somersett litigation and of Sharp's patronage and education of enslaved people in England, it belongs to the evangelical and legalistic attack on the trade, to Sharp's own work as a patron and teacher of freed and abandoned enslaved people in London, and to the wider British argument about personal liberty that ran from the Wilkes controversies to the American dispute.
literary_significance: It supplied the legal and scriptural brief on which later abolitionists built, and its philological appendix anticipated the modern debate over the Bible's servitude texts. As the first substantial English attack on slavery written by a lay patron of the enslaved rather than by a Quaker or a cleric in the colonies, it marks the entry of the question into English public argument about law and conscience.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Granville Sharp is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1769; a second edition with additions appeared in the same year, and the tract is collected in the modern edition of Sharp's antislavery writings edited by William H. and John J. Rives (1985).

title: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade, and of Granting Liberty to the Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies
alternative_titles: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade
description: The book that turned Anglican clerical opinion against the slave trade, written by the Reverend James Ramsay after nineteen years as a surgeon and then a planter's chaplain in Saint Christopher and a rectorate in Kent. Ramsay argues from long residence in the sugar islands that stopping the African trade and gradually freeing the colonial slaves would strengthen rather than ruin the colonies. The Inquiry supplied the abolitionists with first-hand evidence in economic form and made Ramsay the witness whom Wilberforce and the Clapham circle consulted throughout the campaign.
plot_or_argument: Ramsay estimates the numbers of the trade and of the colonial population, then shows that the annual loss of imported Africans must be replaced by costlier purchase and by the constant renewal of a workforce that is worked to death. He next argues that a resident planter and a proportion of free or indentured labour would improve cultivation, that the islands need not be depopulated by emancipation, and that the West Indian interest in the trade is the interest of a few merchants rather than of the colonies. He closes with a gradual scheme: the stop of the importation, the registration and protection of the enslaved, incentives to planters to breed and to treat their people as families, and a progression toward freedom, warning that injustice long tolerated invites judgment upon the nation.
narrative_structure: Single argumentative inquiry in numbered sections combining statistical estimate, case-based description of colonial management, refutation of planter objections and a positive proposal for gradual emancipation.
literary_form: Polemical inquiry in political economy and colonial evidence
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a plain clerical and statistical style, argumentative rather than ornamental
historical_context: Written in the years of the Bristol and Liverpool petitions against the trade, the Somersett precedent and the emerging evangelical humane politics, it answers the planters' claim that abolition would be national ruin and shares the political-arithmetic method of the period's economic writing.
literary_significance: It was the first substantial abolitionist argument built on colonial experience and economic calculation rather than on scripture and sympathy alone, and it converted the question from one of conscience into one of policy. It established the evidential method that Clarkson and Equiano would use and gave the parliamentary campaign its most trusted clerical witness.
attribution_notes: Authorship by James Ramsay is established; the earlier pamphlet letters on the trade are sometimes separately numbered but the Inquiry is his own consolidated argument.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1784; it at once drew a reply from the West India interest and was reprinted in the abolitionist collections of the 1780s. Ramsay's related essays on the colonies appeared in 1785-86.

title: John Bull
alternative_titles: Law is a Bottomless-Pit
description: A political allegory in three letters, published anonymously in 1712 in support of the Harley ministry's peace policy and instantly the most effective piece of war-time argument of its decade. Dr John Arbuthnot turns the Grand Alliance into a family law suit in which John Bull, the plain honest Englishman, has been brought to ruin by trustees, lawyers and a foreign partner. Its homely, low-comic manner made the figure of John Bull the standing personification of the English nation.
plot_or_argument: John Bull, a freeholder of old family, puts his estate in the hands of trustees who hire a foreign partner, Lewis Baboon, and a crew of lawyers and projectors who out-spend the rents, mortgage the land and make John fight to keep what he no longer owns. When John falls into the power of the court of Chancery and the law's bottomless pit, his old servants and neighbours conspire to recover the estate, and the allegory urges the removal of the trustees, the ending of the war and the settlement of the account. Arbuthnot's point is that a people may be enslaved by debt, law and management while believing themselves free.
narrative_structure: Three letters forming a continuous comic allegory, later expanded into a four-part version, with the argument carried by incident and legal farce rather than by direct declamation.
principal_characters: John Bull; Lewis Baboon
literary_form: Political allegory and character tract in epistolary form
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a colloquial, proverb-laden, bunyanesque-narrative register
historical_context: Written during the negotiation of the Preliminaries of the Peace of Utrecht by a physician-close to the Tory ministry and to the Scriblerus circle, it belongs to the ministerial journalism of the Examiner and the Memorials of 1711-12, and to the Scriblerian strategy of using low humour and popular form against the Whig moneyed interest.
literary_significance: It created the national personification that British cartoon and political language used for two centuries, and it is the purest surviving example of Scriblerian political satire in the Augustan public sphere. Its diagnosis of a nation captured by creditors, lawyers and standing armies became a durable idiom for constitutional argument.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; Arbuthnot's authorship was established by his friends' testimony and by the Scriblerus correspondence, and is not now disputed. The later parts and reprints include additions of uncertain extent.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1712, in three letters, the second and third issues following the first within weeks; an enlarged edition appeared the same year and it was reprinted with The Art of Political Lying in several collections of 1712-13.

title: An Essay Concerning the Art of Political Lying
alternative_titles: The Art of Political Lying
description: A short satirical essay in the person of a professor of political lying who reduces mendacity in public affairs to a methodical art with rules, divisions and praise of its practitioners. Dr John Arbuthnot writes in dead-pan mock panegyric, treating falsehood as the great instrument of party, credit and war finance, and the reader supplies the indictment. It is the most perfectly sustained single joke of Scribleran prose and a lasting analysis of how political language works.
plot_or_argument: The narrator first compliments his age on the perfection to which the art of lying has been brought, then divides political lying into species, including the proof-lie, the lie of the first and second figure, the offence-defensive lie, and the equivoque, each illustrated by public practice. He next argues that the art is essential to party management, to the support of public funds and to the conduct of a war that must be concealed from the people who pay for it. He claims the greatest masters of the art for his own party's opponents while complimenting all sides, and ends with the modest proposal that a college or society should be founded for the better cultivation of the science.
narrative_structure: Continuous mock-institutional essay, organised as panegyric, taxonomy of the species, application to current practice, and closing project.
literary_form: Satirical essay and character in the mock-didactic manner
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a level, ironical, precept-giving Augustan plain style
historical_context: Published in the last months of the Harley ministry's attack on the Whig moneyed interest, amid the Examiner and Scriblerus campaign against party falsehood, stock-jobbing and the news-peddling of the addresses. It presupposes the 1711-12 debates over the public funds and the conduct of the war.
literary_significance: It gave the Augustan vocabulary a durable name for organised public untruth and remains the standard early analysis of political spin. Its method, a taxonomy built wholly out of irony, became a model for later satirists from Cobbett to the twentieth-century mock manual, and it is the clearest non-Popean expression of the Scribleran war against dullness and imposture.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Arbuthnot in the Scriblerus collections and accepted by modern scholarship; it was sometimes placed among Swift's pieces in early collected editions, which accounts for the older doubt.
bibliographical_notes: First published as a single pamphlet, London, printed by John Morphew, 1712, and soon reprinted in miscellanies and in editions of Arbuthnot's and Swift's works.

title: The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus
alternative_titles: Memoirs of Martinus Scriblerus
Memoirs of the extraordinary Life, Works, and Discoveries of Martinus Scriblerus
description: The collected issue, in two volumes, of the papers of the Scriblerus club, printed seven years after Arbuthnot's death and four after Swift's and Parnell's. Its centrepiece is the Memoirs of the imaginary pedant Martinus Scriblerus, a burlesque life and catalogue of false discoveries, accompanied by the club's earlier pieces against false learning, bad taste and the abuse of scholarship. The volume is the published monument of the greatest joint satirical project of the Augustan age.
plot_or_argument: The Memoirs recount how Martinus, the posthumous son of a great man, is educated by a circle of projectors who teach him every system of error: false philosophy, obsolete scholarship, the art of digging for hidden treasure, and the machinery of pedantic invention. Thereupon he devotes his vast industry to useless discoveries, among them a treatise on the shadow of a bat and a mechanical device for travelling by pinning the wind, and ends in a universal scheme of knowledge that teaches everything and signifies nothing. The accompanying tracts attack the modern critick, the moneyed interest and the corrupt clergy, converting the club's private jests into a public indictment of learning without sense and of wit in the service of dullness.
narrative_structure: Miscellany: a Mock-biographical Memoirs in continuous narrative, followed by separately titled essays, eclogues, notes and pieces of club origin, with an apparatus of fabricated scholarship.
principal_characters: Martinus Scriblerus; his tutors and projectors; the club's personae of invented editors
literary_form: Collaborative satirical miscellany: mock-biography, mock-didactic essay, eclogue and parodic scholarly apparatus
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose in a parodic latinised period style, with interspersed Hudibrastic and Augustan verse pieces
historical_context: Drawn up during the club's Oxford and London meetings of roughly 1710-1714 and assembled for the press in the literary quarrels of the 1730s, the volume reflects the Scribleran campaign against the criticks, the projectors and the Whig learning of the age, and Pope's use of club material in the Dunciad.
literary_significance: It fixed the type of the pedant and of organised dullness for two centuries and is the foundational document of Augustan collaboration. Its model of satire as a joint construction of fictitious scholarship runs directly from here through Fielding, Sterne and the nineteenth-century mock-book, and it remains the best evidence of the Scriblerans' theory that ridicule is the test of imposture.
attribution_notes: Club composition: the shares of John Arbuthnot, Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift and John Gay, with Thomas Parnell and Bishop Atterbury, are much debated and cannot be assigned with confidence; the Memoirs are chiefly Arbuthnot's with Pope's revision, and the 1741 text was prepared with Pope's involvement. Recorded here as a single collaborative volume, with the four principal club members credited in the map.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1741, two volumes, under the title The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus, the Memoirs forming the second volume; the standard scholarly edition is Lewis Theobald's text as reprinted in The Prose Works of Martinus Scriblerus, ed. C. B. Anderson (1969).

title: Essays on the Active Powers of Man
description: The second half of Thomas Reid's planned division of the human mind, published in Edinburgh in 1788 after the Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Its seven essays analyse what a person does rather than what a person knows: agency, will, motive and freedom, conscience, the moral power, and the authority of the understanding over conduct. It is the mature statement of the common-sense school's philosophy of action and of its defence of liberty against Hume and Hartley.
plot_or_argument: Reid begins by distinguishing active power from mere event, arguing that the very notion of cause is drawn from our consciousness of our own agency. He then examines the will, motive and the relation of volition to desire, and maintains that a free agent is an efficient cause whose choices are determined by neither necessity nor the strongest motive. The following essays treat moral agency, the conscience as a judge pronouncing upon character and not only upon actions, and the principles of action in brute animals and in human art and science. Finally Reid argues that sound judgment, or common sense, governs practice as much as belief, so that the same original principles which direct the understanding direct conduct.
narrative_structure: Seven sequential essays of analytical moral psychology, advancing from the analysis of agency to the will, moral obligation, conscience and the governance of common sense in action.
literary_form: Analytical treatise in moral philosophy, essay by essay
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a plain, patient, lecture-derived analytical style
historical_context: Written in the last Aberdeen and Edinburgh decades of Reid's life, after the Intellectual Powers and amid the controversy over Humean necessity and Priestley's materialism, it belongs to the Scottish Enlightenment's systematic reconstruction of the faculties and to the Common-Sense school's debate with the physiology of Hartley.
literary_significance: It is the principal eighteenth-century defence of human liberty and of the moral sense against sceptical analysis, and the source of Reid's influential account of conscience as a judicial faculty. Its philosophy of action, largely neglected in its own century, has been recovered by recent work on agency and free will, and it completes the Common-Sense programme that shaped Reid's American disciples.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Thomas Reid is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1788; reprinted with the Intellectual Powers in the collected Works of 1792, which carries Beattie's memoir, and in William H. Duggan's edition (1967-69). The essays were long in preparation and their composition cannot be dated year by year.

title: Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty, the Principles of Government, and the Justice and Policy of the Mother Country, respecting the Colonies
alternative_titles: Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty
description: The pamphlet that made the Unitarian minister Richard Price the most read political writer of the American crisis. Issued in London in early 1776 and running through many editions within months, it argues from the first principles of civil liberty that the colonies cannot lawfully be taxed without consent, and that a free people's relation to the mother country must be that of voluntary allegiance, not of subordinate taxation. Its cool arithmetic of empire and its appeal to the reason of the reader made it more influential in America than most American writing of the same year.
plot_or_argument: Price first defines civil liberty as the right of a people to make their own laws, and asserts that this cannot be delegated or lost, so that no legislature may bind those it does not represent. He examines the constitutional history of the colonies, their charters and their practice of self-taxation, and concludes that Parliament's claim to legislate for them in all cases whatsoever is an assumption never consented to. He then weighs the policy of the mother country, arguing that trade and affection, not force, hold an empire together, and that an overgrown state tends toward despotism. Finally he urges accommodation, warning that coercion will produce the very independence it seeks and that Britain's true interest lies in justice.
narrative_structure: Continuous argumentative pamphlet in numbered sections moving from principles to constitutional case, commercial policy and counsel of accommodation.
literary_form: Political pamphlet and treatise on liberty and empire
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a plain, reasoned, sermon-clean style of short paragraphs and rhetorical questions
historical_context: Written between the Olive Branch Petition and the Declaration of Independence amid the British debate over American policy, it belongs to the Dissenting commonwealth tradition, to the Whig opposition of Rockingham and Chatham, and to the print boom of the crisis, when pamphlets were reprinted across the Atlantic within weeks.
literary_significance: It supplied the most rigorous British statement of the colonial case and helped convert the argument from taxation into one about representation and the nature of consent, anticipating Paine and shaping American reading of the Declaration. As the work of a London Dissenting minister it also shows the transmission of the British radical tradition into revolutionary America, and its warning about overgrown states became a permanent element of Anglo-American republican language.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Richard Price is established and undisputed, though early editions circulated under the cover of anonymity while his name was common knowledge.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1776; several editions and printings appeared in that year, including reprints in the colonies, and the pamphlet was answered in a series of ministerial replies. A modern scholarly reprint appears in David S. Katz's edition, Richard Price: Political Writings (1991).

title: Disquisitions relating to Matter and Spirit
description: The philosophical statement of Joseph Priestley's unitarian materialism, published in London in 1777 and gathering his earlier controversy with the Scottish common-sense school into a positive doctrine. Priestley argues that mind is a property of organised matter, that the soul is not naturally immortal, and that the Christian hope is resurrection rather than an intermediate state of separate spirits. Its combination of physiology, necessity and biblical criticism made it, in contemporary judgment, the most dangerous of his writings.
plot_or_argument: Priestley first examines the evidence of consciousness and of physiology, and concludes that thought, memory and desire are inseparable from the brain, so that an immaterial thinking substance is an unintelligible hypothesis. He then defends philosophical necessity, arguing that the will is determined by the strongest motive and that virtue and happiness advance by the same mechanism of association which Hartley had described. Against Reid, Beattie and Oswald he denies innate ideas and the authority of common sense in metaphysics, insisting that all belief is built on experience and testimony. Finally he turns to Scripture and shows that the hope of the Bible is a resurrection of the body, that the wicked are destroyed rather than tormented for ever, and that the popular philosophy of the soul supports a corrupt religion of selfishness.
narrative_structure: Composite treatise of disquisitions and reprinted controversy, advancing from physiology and the will through the critique of common-sense metaphysics to a scriptural theology of resurrection.
literary_form: Philosophical and theological disquisition in polemic form
meter_and_prosody: Prose only, in a blunt, businesslike, argumentative Nonconformist style
historical_context: Written in the Birmingham circle's long controversy with the Scottish school and with the Evangelical Revival, and in the aftermath of Priestley's Hartleian physiology and his founding of unitarian theology, it belongs to the materialist and necessitarian current of the English Enlightenment and to the Dissenting attack on the popular doctrine of hell.
literary_significance: It is the boldest English attempt to found a religion on matter, necessity and association, and it set the terms of the nineteenth-century debate over the soul in which its opponents were obliged to answer its physiology as well as its exegesis. Its defence of the mortalist reading of Scripture remains a reference point in the history of heterodox theology, and its psychology influenced the associationist and utilitarian tradition.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Joseph Priestley is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1777, for J. Johnson; it incorporated his earlier Examination of Dr. Reid, Dr. Beattie and Dr. Oswald and drew an immediate stream of replies, and a second edition appeared in 1782.
